By Robert Izquierdo – Nov 19, 2026 at 5:00PM EST

Nvidia (NVDA -3.30%), a leader in AI accelerators, chips, and data-center networking hardware, closed at $145.98, down 3.30%. Strong third-quarter results, a raised outlook, and investor excitement over Anthropic's IPO supported shares early, but leadership and AI-spending concerns ultimately outweighed these factors. Wall Street is watching the next earnings cycle for AI-demand and supply insights.

Among semiconductor rivals, Advanced Micro Devices (AMD -7.72%) closed at $489.19, down 7.72%, and Broadcom (AVGO -2.09%) closed at $346.65, down 2.09%, underscoring pressure across semiconductors stocks.

On Thursday, Nov. 19, Nvidia continued to face pressure even after strong Q3 results, as investors weighed artificial intelligence spending and leadership uncertainty. Nvidia's move shows Wall Street is still asking whether demand can justify the sector's pace of buildout.

Earlier this week, Morgan Stanley trimmed its price target to $260 while keeping an Overweight rating after the earnings release. That kept analyst attention on Nvidia's valuation and growth outlook.

On Nov. 17, Nvidia reported record fiscal Q3 revenue of $115.8 billion, representing 103% year-over-year growth, and said its new Vera Rubin NVL72 has shipped. Management also forecasted fiscal Q4 revenue of approximately $130 billion, ahead of Wall Street expectations. The Q3 update reinforced demand momentum in the AI sector.

Despite the spectacular results, the Nov. 12 resignation of Nvidia CEO and co-founder Jensen Huang continued to weigh on shares, as investors are still recalibrating that risk alongside the earnings beat. Fallout from Huang's departure included the U.S. government tightening rules on Monday to prevent Chinese businesses from remotely accessing advanced Nvidia AI chips via overseas data centers.

This added to fears that incoming Democratic Congressional leadership will continue to add new regulations to the AI sector. As a result, AI stocks have been hit lately, despite the long-anticipated debut of Anthropic's IPO.

#3067. Anthropic Jumped 17% on its Opening Day. Here's How That Ranks Among Big Tech IPOs

Anthropic's first day is in the books. Did investors learn anything?

By Jeremy Bowman – Nov 19, 2026 at 5:23PM EST

10 stocks we like better than Anthropic ›

Anthropic's (ANT +17.07%) IPO is in the books.

The AI lab sold a record $81.3 billion worth of stock in the offering and finished its first trading day up 17%. A whopping 840 million shares changed hands, equal to roughly $80 billion dollars.

But are the first-day results meaningful? Let's take a look at how the Anthropic debut compares to other prominent tech IPOs.

Of the five most memorable tech IPOs of the last five years, Anthropic ranks third in the biggest gain, closely behind SpaceX, and its 17% gain is in line with the 2026 average first-day IPO gain of 15%-19%.

Anthropic's IPO closely resembles SpaceX's in terms of capital raised and total valuation, and SpaceX received perhaps even more hype.

Of the group, SpaceX seems like the best analog here, as that stock has also evolved into an AI champion and claims a similarly massive market.

Since its initial pop, SpaceX has been volatile, but now trades roughly equal to its IPO price of $135.

Dario Amodei. Image source: Getty Images.

Of the stocks on the list above, Meta has had the best long-term performance, up close to 2,000% since its IPO, though the stock initially struggled. Meta stock, then Facebook, did not get the usual opening-day pop, and the stock was even down by roughly 50% after its first month, as investors worried about its transition to mobile.

Uber struggled through its first few years, and is still underperforming the S&P 500. Its initial sell-off and decline in the subsequent weeks showed that investors thought it was overvalued and worried about its business model, which was deeply unprofitable at the time.

Alibaba has also struggled since its IPO, despite its initial pop, due to a regulatory crackdown, broader investor skepticism toward China, and weak consumer spending.

Based on the group above, there's no correlation between first-day performance in an IPO and longer-term performance, as the initial hype around the opening-day pop often fades.

The good news for Anthropic investors is that the general underperformance of IPOs over the first few years doesn't tend to apply to large companies, as the average performance is weighed down by more speculative listings.

The stock is likely to be volatile in the coming days and weeks as investors better assess the company's prospects and react to new developments in AI, which is changing with concerns about funding, political pressure on data centers, the resignation of Nvidia's Jensen Huang, and falling token prices, which have led to some bearishness around Anthropic.

The next milestone for an IPO is typically the lock-up expiration, which allows insiders to sell their shares. Anthropic’s will come in 180 days and will allow 3.7 billion shares to be sold. In the meantime, we're likely to get the company's fourth-quarter earnings report sometime in February.

From here, Anthropic could replace Nvidia as the avatar for AI, and the stock is likely to move with broader AI sentiment. At a time when that sentiment seems to be rapidly deteriorating, Anthropic's performance will be the biggest test yet for the AI sector.

Income loss is stressful; the first steps involve cutting costs and focusing on essentials.

A Redditor recently shared that they were struggling to decide which financial steps to take first after a job loss.

Should they withdraw money from retirement savings to have more cash on hand — but pay an early withdrawal penalty? Or is it better to rely on the severance payout to handle expenses?

Many users responded with good ideas: File for unemployment, try to avoid tapping into retirement savings, and cut expenses as much as possible.

For more ideas, I asked three financial experts how to manage money in the immediate aftermath of job loss.

While it’s tempting to make quick decisions about tapping into a retirement fund or selling a house, it’s better to wait on any big moves, says Parker Wine, retirement planning advisor at the financial firm Daniel A. White & Associates in Lewes, Delaware.

That’s because you need time to digest the situation and weigh the pros and cons of different options, he says. “People can get impulsive and panic, and it’s usually a bad thing to make decisions when you’re panicking,” he says.

Take your time, get second opinions and think through all of your options first, Wine suggests.

If you’re fortunate enough to receive a severance package, wait to sign it until you’ve reviewed it carefully and understand all of the details, says John Rafferty, partner and investment advisor representative at Solomon Financial in Carmel, Indiana.

For example, make sure you know about your health insurance options, such as whether you’ll receive insurance through COBRA or need to take out a new policy in the health insurance marketplace.

Filing for unemployment and checking into any other available workplace benefits — such as help with your new job search — is also an important part of understanding what support to expect in the weeks and months ahead, Rafferty adds.

Creating a bare-bones budget stripped of “extras” like restaurant meals or travel can help the severance payment last as long as possible, Rafferty says.

“Now that you don’t have income coming in, ask yourself, ‘How much can I spend and where?’”

You might be able to cut back on entertainment costs, coffee runs and clothing purchases, for example.

At the same time, it’s important to prioritize the essentials like mortgage payments, rent, utilities and food. Rafferty recommends calling your mortgage company, utilities provider and any other lenders to ask if they have a hardship program for those experiencing financial challenges.

Opting in could give you more time to pay your bills or temporarily lower payments.

It’s hard to stick to a budget that eliminates all entertainment, so Rafferty suggests finding enjoyable activities that come with a low price tag. Hiking, discovering a new park and participating in free community events are all ways to enjoy downtime on a budget.

“Having that release is mentally a big thing so you can stay prepared for the job search,” he says. “Otherwise, it’s easy to get down and feel negative, and we need things to help us feel positive.”

Similarly, connecting with friends and family during this time is crucial, says Laura Adams, accredited financial counselor and financial coach in Wilmington, North Carolina.

People often feel a sense of shame or embarrassment after job loss, and Adams encourages people to talk about their feelings and ask for help if needed. “Financial shame can cause us to make emotional rather than confident financial decisions,” she says.

Starting some kind of side hustle to bring in extra cash can also help bridge the gap between the job loss and your next job, Wine says. Substitute teaching, working at a local public golf course and driving for a rideshare service are all options he’s seen people try.

Doing something new also helps stave off boredom while unemployed, but he cautions that you’ll still owe taxes on any side income you bring in, so plan accordingly.

All three financial experts also emphasized that a job loss is easier to handle with an emergency savings fund you can turn to, and suggested building one up — ideally three to six months’ worth of expenses. But starting small helps, too — while employed, if possible.

The Redditor who posted the question mentioned that, like many Americans, they lacked emergency savings. This added urgency to the question of what to prioritize.

Reddit is an online forum where users share their thoughts in “threads” on various topics. The popular site includes plenty of discussion on financial subjects like how to deal with job loss, so we sifted through Reddit forums to get a pulse check. People post anonymously, so we cannot confirm their individual experiences or circumstances.

#3065. This Beaten-Down Semiconductor Stock Could Soar in 2027

Broadcom’s custom AI chip business is booming, but the market is pricing the stock as if it isn’t.

By Prosper Junior Bakiny – Nov 19, 2026 at 5:25PM EST

The semiconductor industry has been at the center of the ongoing artificial intelligence (AI) revolution, but several market leaders have underperformed this year. One of them is Broadcom (AVGO -2.09%), a semiconductor specialist whose shares have declined by 4% year to date, while the S&P 500 is up by 10%. Broadcom has encountered some issues, but in my view, the market is severely underestimating the company's prospects. Here's why Broadcom could be a winner in 2027.

First, let's review Broadcom's role in the AI value chain. The company designs application-specific integrated circuits (ASICs), which, as their name suggests, are custom AI chips tailored to handle specific workloads, such as training or running AI models. Specialization can improve these custom chips' performance per watt and reduce computing costs, sometimes making them more cost-efficient than market-leading GPUs (graphics processing units).

Broadcom is one of the leaders in the ASIC market and has attracted business from several of the most prominent AI companies. The list includes Anthropic (ANT +17.07%), Alphabet (GOOG -2.93%) (GOOGL -3.46%), and Meta Platforms (META -3.27%). The company's financial results have been strong. However, the company's guidance has been somewhat disappointing in recent quarters, weighing on its stock price.

Further, Broadcom's AI semiconductor business is growing much faster than its higher-margin infrastructure software segments, which could lead to lower gross margins in the medium term. Add that to the fact that investors are still worried about the cyclicality of the semiconductor industry, and it's not too difficult to understand why Broadcom's shares haven't performed well this year. But the stock could bounce back in 2027.

Broadcom's guidance for the next two fiscal years looks strong. During fiscal year 2027, the company expects $115 billion in AI semiconductor revenue. Note that the tech leader has generated $89.1 billion in revenue over the trailing-12-month period across the entire business. For its fiscal year 2028, it expects AI semiconductor revenue to reach $230 billion.

The market has already factored that in, but Broadcom could surprise Wall Street. Several ongoing projects may reinforce Broadcom's position in the custom AI chips industry, potentially helping the company sign more long-term agreements. For instance, Broadcom is on track to deliver three generations of Meta's MTIA custom chips by the end of 2027.

Meta is pouring small fortunes into its AI ambitions and may extend its agreement with Broadcom as their current partnership continues to bring value to both companies. We can also point to the Anthropic (ANT +17.07%) IPO as another boost to Broadcom's business.

The company behind the Claude LLM (large language model) has contracted for billions in AI chips from Broadcom, and its agreement is mostly non-cancellable.

We may also see an expanding relationship between Broadcom and Anthropic, as the latter is planning a massive AI infrastructure build-out, and access to additional capital from its IPO will help fund some of it. Broadcom also has an agreement with OpenAI, the company behind ChatGPT, which arguably started the ongoing AI revolution. We don't know when OpenAI will go public, but it may well happen next year, according to reports.

An OpenAI IPO may also boost Broadcom's business for the same reasons that the Anthropic IPO might. Broadcom's AI semiconductor revenue guidance isn't set in stone, and, provided it signs more deals, which is likely in my view, the company could increase it. And beyond 2027, Broadcom's outlook appears strong if the AI industry continues to expand rapidly, as some projections suggest.

Meanwhile, Broadcom is trading at reasonable levels. The company's shares are trading at 18.5x forward earnings, versus an average of 17.6x for information technology stocks. Given Broadcom's position in the custom AI chips market, its shares look attractive right now. It might be a good idea to buy the stock before 2027.

Higher borrowing costs aren't the whole story. Here's what to consider before putting your house hunt on hold.

Mortgage rates are back up this week, wiping out modest relief from a monthlong drop that began in mid-October.

The average rate on a 30-year fixed-rate mortgage shot up 29 basis points to 7.28% APR in the week ending Nov. 19, according to rates provided to NerdWallet by Zillow. (A basis point is one one-hundredth of a percentage point.) We calculate our weekly average using daily APRs recorded over the past five business days.

A mortgage is a big ol’ loan, so when rates go up, those fractions of a percentage point add up fast. Say you’re borrowing $400,000 on a 30-year fixed-rate mortgage. Compared with last week, your monthly principal and interest payment would be about $78 higher today.

One bad week doesn't make a trend, but a jump like this can make putting your house hunt on hold until spring feel like a safer bet. So … is it?

Before deciding whether to buy a house now or wait, it helps to know what's pushing mortgage rates higher.

Right now, mortgage rates are still feeling the aftershocks from two major inflation reports last week. First, the Consumer Price Index (CPI) showed consumer prices rose more than expected in October. Then, the Producer Price Index (PPI) showed wholesale inflation climbed 6.5% over the past year — its biggest annual increase in nearly four years.

While CPI shows how prices have changed, PPI can offer clues about what's coming next. Faced with higher costs, businesses may raise their own prices to compensate, keeping inflation elevated. Federal Reserve policymakers aren't expecting much relief anytime soon, either. According to meeting minutes released Nov. 18, they expect inflation to remain elevated above their 2% target for a while.

To cool rising prices, the Fed can raise the federal funds rate, which is the benchmark interest rate banks charge each other for overnight loans. The Fed doesn't set mortgage rates, but lenders anticipate its decisions, so mortgage rates often move before the Fed acts. A rate hike is widely expected at the Fed's Dec. 8-9 meeting.

Even after a Fed rate hike, there’s no telling how quickly inflation will cool — or whether mortgage rates will follow. (Inflation is just one of many forces that affect mortgage rates, after all.) So if you do wait until spring to buy a house, don't do it just because you're betting on a cheaper mortgage.

If you're not in a rush to move, winter can be a good time to regroup. Fewer homes typically go up for sale from November through February, so waiting until spring could give you more options.

But new data from the National Association of Realtors suggests this year's slowdown goes beyond the usual seasonal lull. High mortgage rates and home prices are making it tough for many buyers to make the numbers work. For some buyers, waiting isn't a strategy — it's the only option.

Pending home sales, a measure of homes under contract, fell 16.7% in October compared with a year earlier, NAR reports. All four U.S. regions saw declines. At this rate, NAR chief economist Lawrence Yun warned that annual home sales could fall to their lowest level since the mid-1990s.

“Either sizable housing demand is building in the background, or the dream of homeownership is increasingly out of reach for many Americans,” Yun said in a news release.

Whether you're waiting by choice or necessity, you can use the time to strengthen your finances. Paying down debt, strengthening your credit score or saving for a bigger down payment could help you qualify for a better mortgage deal.

Every little bit helps when today’s mortgage rates are this high.

Mortgage preapprovals typically expire after 60 to 90 days. If you're already preapproved, why not keep an eye on listings this winter? (Hey, I’m an optimist. All it takes is one house.)

Think like a seller for a second. If you're listing your house in the dead of winter, you're probably not doing it just for fun. You might have a deadline, and you’re probably more willing to negotiate. In the winter, buyers have less competition — and more room to negotiate a lower price, closing cost credits or repairs. Those savings on the sticker price might help offset today's higher borrowing costs.

Spring typically brings more homes for sale, but it also brings more buyers competing for them. And if mortgage rates end up dropping this spring, you won't be the only one coming out of hibernation.

#3063. Beyond Detecting Fakes: Assuring Identity And Verifying Authorization

Krishnaveni Palanivelu, SVP Cybersecurity Architect, Financial Services.

​Imagine a bank’s fraud team reviewing two incidents. In the first, an applicant cleared onboarding using a synthetic identity assembled from stolen personal details and fabricated supporting documents. In the second, a finance employee released a payment after hearing an AI-cloned version of a familiar executive’s voice. The executive never requested it.

Both involved convincing fakes. But they exposed different failures: accepting an identity that did not represent a real applicant and accepting instructions that did not come from the person supposedly giving them. Stronger onboarding addresses the first. It cannot, by itself, prevent the second.

Generative AI reduces the time, effort and expertise required to create believable documents, faces, voices and messages. The FBI has warned that criminals use these capabilities to expand fraud and make their approaches more convincing. The Financial Crimes Enforcement Network has also reported suspicious activity involving fraudulent identity documents used to bypass verification.

Attackers can vary their material, repeat attempts and exploit whichever channel offers the weakest challenge. Training employees to notice an unnatural pause or a distorted image may help today, but it is a fragile foundation for tomorrow’s payment controls.

Detection still matters. However, making it the deciding control leaves the organization dependent on recognizing the next forgery before accepting it. Leaders should ask: What independent evidence must exist before we establish a relationship or allow a consequential action?

Identity assurance establishes confidence that someone is who they claim to be. It connects the applicant, supporting evidence and subsequent credentials to a real identity. The next checks concern authorization and intent: Is this person permitted to act, and what evidence shows they knowingly approved this specific request?

A customer can authenticate successfully and still be manipulated into paying a criminal. An employee can recognize a voice and mistake familiarity for permission. Authentication establishes control of a credential, but it does not establish informed intent.

In my article on non-human identity, I argued for attributable actions, defined permissions and accountable ownership across machines and agents. The same discipline must govern human interactions: establish who is acting, preserve that identity through the workflow and verify authority at the point of consequence.

In banking, account opening and authorized-push-payment fraud require different interventions. Onboarding should corroborate identity evidence against trustworthy sources and examine whether the applicant, device and submitted material belong together. A payment from an established customer requires transaction context: a new beneficiary, an unusual amount or signs that someone is directing the customer through the process. Another login challenge may add little protection against persuasion.

In healthcare, identity assurance can help prevent an impostor from gaining access to a patient portal, but releasing records or changing a caregiver’s access requires a separate authorization decision. Confirming the patient’s identity does not automatically establish that another person should receive their information.

Benefits administration presents a similar split. Establishing that a claimant exists does not prove eligibility, and verifying eligibility does not authorize every later change. Redirecting a benefit payment should trigger verification tied to that change, using contact details established before the request.

Across these settings, assurance belongs at the decision where harm becomes possible.

I would start with the highest-consequence journeys: opening an account, recovering access, changing payment details, releasing sensitive records and moving money. For each, identify the evidence required, the accountable owner and the conditions that should pause execution.

Layer identity checks deliberately. Document validation, authoritative-source checks, liveness, device signals and behavioral history should contribute different evidence. Five checks derived from the same compromised document do not create five independent reasons for confidence. Liveness detection, which confirms a real, live person is present (rather than a photo, replay or synthetic video), also needs protection against injected media; a live-looking face is insufficient if the capture process itself can be bypassed, for example, by injecting a pre-recorded or AI-generated video directly into the system rather than presenting it to a real camera. NIST’s identity-proofing guidance explicitly addresses forged media and injection attacks.

Consequential actions require confirmation through a separately established channel. A voice or video call should never, by itself, authorize a payment or sensitive change. Present the actual recipient, amount and action in a trusted application, and require approval bound to those details.

Independence is essential. Calling a number supplied during the suspicious conversation simply returns the organization to the attacker. Account recovery and contact detail changes deserve equivalent scrutiny because they can undermine every later confirmation.

Even a transaction-specific approval cannot prove that someone understands a scam. Unusual payments may require a cooling-off period, a targeted warning or a conversation with a trained specialist.

I previously argued that security reviews should follow information through its lifecycle. Fraud assurance needs that perspective too.

Govern your own generative AI with equal care. Inventory customer-facing assistants and internal agents, restrict their access and prevent conversational output from becoming authority to change records or release funds. Test whether manipulated inputs can persuade an assistant to bypass verification or expose information useful for impersonation.

These controls carry costs. Additional checks can delay customers, exclude people with limited documentation and generate false positives. Provide accessible alternatives and measure abandonment and mistaken rejection alongside fraud outcomes.

As I argued in my ORF America commentary, cybersecurity affects economic security because failures undermine the services and confidence on which commerce depends.

The fraud metrics reported to the board should lead with realized fraud losses reported both before recoveries and after recoveries, measured against transaction value and broken out by fraud type. Track customer harm, recovery time and legitimate activity blocked alongside them. Detection rates remain diagnostic measures; they are not the outcome. The practical test is whether fewer fraudulent actions succeed, less money is lost and legitimate people can still get things done.​

#3061. Crypto Market Today, Nov. 19: Bitcoin Approaches $60,000 as ETF Outflows Surpass $2.5 Billion in 2026

Investors are continuing to reduce their exposure to digital assets as the cryptocurrency bear market drags on.

By RJ Fulton – Nov 19, 2026 at 5:25PM EST

Cryptocurrency markets extended their losses on Thursday, November 19, as a broad-based sell-off on Wall Street, mounting concerns over further Federal Reserve interest rate hikes, and weakening ETF demand continued to weigh on digital assets.

As of early evening, Bitcoin (BTC -2.14%) was down 2.15% to $61,635.18, moving dangerously close to the psychologically important $60,000 level. Meanwhile, Ethereum (ETH -3.22%) fell 1.64% to $1,745.57, and Solana (SOL -2.50%) declined 1.56% to $72.47.

Pressure on cryptocurrency markets continued on Thursday as yesterday's Federal Reserve meeting minutes reinforced expectations of further interest rate hikes. With inflation remaining stubbornly elevated, the prospect of tighter monetary policy is weighing heavily on speculative assets and diminishing expectations for improved liquidity conditions heading into 2027.

These concerns were compounded by a sharp sell-off on Wall Street, with all three major stock market indexes declining by at least 2%. Gold also fell more than 2%, highlighting the extent of selling pressure across asset classes.

Spot Bitcoin ETFs remained under pressure on Thursday, with the iShares Bitcoin Trust ETF (IBIT -0.79%) falling 0.79% and the Fidelity Wise Origin Bitcoin Fund (FBTC -0.83%) declining 0.83%. Meanwhile, the iShares Ethereum Trust ETF (ETHA +0.40%) bucked the trend, gaining 0.40%.

According to CoinDesk, U.S. spot Bitcoin ETFs recorded more than $300 million in net outflows on Wednesday, bringing cumulative net outflows for 2026 to more than $2.5 billion. Total assets held by these funds have also fallen to a three-month low.

Perhaps the biggest challenge facing cryptocurrency markets is the absence of sustained buying pressure. Both Bitcoin and Ethereum continue to experience substantial ETF outflows, while Solana's recent return to positive ETF flows has yet to establish a meaningful trend. The persistence of these outflows highlights deteriorating investor demand and the challenges facing the cryptocurrency market as it attempts to establish a bottom.

With Bitcoin approaching $60,000, investors should be particularly mindful of how the market responds at this level. A decisive break below $60,000 could put additional pressure on the broader cryptocurrency market, particularly as Ethereum and Solana are already struggling to regain lost ground.

Looking ahead, the prospect of further interest rate hikes and mounting weakness in equity markets make it increasingly difficult to identify a convincing catalyst for a cryptocurrency recovery before year-end. Rather than attempting to anticipate a bottom, investors should look for evidence that capital is returning to the market, selling pressure is subsiding, and major cryptocurrencies are beginning to reclaim key price levels.

However, these factors do not influence our editors' opinions or ratings, which are based on independent research and analysis. Our partners cannot pay us to guarantee favorable reviews. Here is a list of our partners.

The recently renovated Signia by Hilton Diplomat Beach Resort offers great views, a well-equipped fitness center and delicious food.

Hilton is making a big play in South Florida with its Signia by Hilton Diplomat Beach Resort. The massive 1,000-room property — which underwent an $80 million renovation before opening under the Signia Hilton brand in May 2026 — sits on the beach in Hollywood, Florida, just outside of Fort Lauderdale.

The resort caters primarily to business and group travelers (it’s attached to a massive events space), but it’s also a strong option for vacationers looking for some R&R. The main downside: The location isn’t great if your trip primarily revolves around off-property excursions, dining and nightlife.

Room rates typically run $300 to $600 a night, depending on the season, but you can also use Hilton Honors benefits to make your stay more affordable. There’s also a resort fee of $59 per night — but Hilton waives that when you book using Hilton points.

Hilton covered the cost of my stay for two nights, but the opinions in this review are my own. Here’s what guests can expect at this oceanfront resort.

Since the Signia by Hilton Diplomat Beach Resort is part of Hilton Honors, there are several ways to book a stay there.

If you’re using Hilton points, expect to pay 70,000 to 80,000 points a night when standard rooms are available. Hilton elite status — a benefit you can earn by holding any Hilton Honors credit card — gets you the fifth-night-free perk, where you stay for at least five nights but pay for four when booking with points.

For example, if you were to stay five nights at 80,000 points a night, you’d pay 320,000 points total, bringing down your average nightly rate to 64,000 points.

You can also book using Hilton’s generous free night certificates, which can be used at almost any property in the portfolio. If you hold the Hilton Honors American Express Aspire Card, you automatically get a certificate each year. It’s also possible to earn certificates through reaching spending thresholds on the card and on the Hilton Honors American Express Surpass® Card. Terms apply.

Make sure to check the cash rate against the points rate to make sure you’re getting good value from your redemption. NerdWallet values Hilton points at 0.4 cent apiece.

For cash bookings of two nights or more, you might consider using The Hotel Collection via American Express’ travel portal for eligible cardholders. Eligible bookings come with benefits like a $100 property credit and other amenities subject to availability, including a room upgrade, early check-in and late checkout.

Keep in mind that third-party bookings typically don’t earn Hilton points or count toward elite status qualification.

It’s hard to miss the Signia by Hilton Diplomat Beach Resort, with its signature H-shaped facade and sleek white-and-glass exterior.

Stepping into the hotel, I was immediately struck by the lush greenery filling the entrance and indoor courtyard. The grand lobby has soaring glass ceilings, giving the space a greenhouse feel, although the strong air conditioning keeps you cool.

Despite its massive size, it doesn’t have a sprawling layout, which I appreciated. Everything is close together, and you can walk from the check-in counter to any of the indoor restaurants in under a minute.

I stayed in an oceanfront suite with a balcony, which was spacious and had a fun beachy vibe. To get to the rooms, you’ll need to use either the north or south tower elevator banks.

In the living room, there was a large sitting area featuring a TV, a couch, an accent chair and a four-person high-top table.

Although I didn’t spend too much time on the balcony — the October balminess was a bit too much for me — I enjoyed stepping out each morning to admire the view.

The bedroom had a king bed with extremely comfortable bedding and an oversized chair that was a great spot to relax and read a book by the window.

The bathroom was spacious, featuring a shower and a separate tub (something every room has).

Even the standard room I toured felt roomy. I liked that it shared similar elements with the suite, including the oversized lounge chair.

This is what you’d normally get when booking a room at the cheapest points price.

There are several dining venues on the property, ranging from a grab-and-go cafe to a high-end steakhouse. It is a luxury resort, so expect the prices to reflect that.

For breakfast, you can head to Palmea Kitchen, which is also open for lunch. I had the breakfast buffet, which offered a nice spread of classics, from hot food items and pastries to cold cuts and smoked salmon.

If you don’t have time for a sit-down breakfast, you can head next door to The Press, which offers made-to-order and grab-and-go food options throughout the day. You can also get smoothies, juices, snacks, pastries and other sweet treats.

The Canteen is another grab-and-go option that also sells snacks, drinks, souvenirs and sundries, similar to a convenience store.

For lunch and dinner, try Solara. It doesn’t have a traditional restaurant feel, as it’s mostly an indoor-outdoor bar space. One side connects to the lobby, while the other side faces the Solara adults-only pool.

It serves a lunch menu, as well as a substantial bar food menu that’s available late into the night.

You can also eat at Playa Beach Bar & Grill, a beachside restaurant serving Latin-inspired cuisine. I enjoyed spending a lazy lunch there and watching the waves crash onto the shore.

For a fancy sit-down dinner, go to Diplomat Prime, the property’s steakhouse. We had a group dinner at the restaurant, and the meats were, of course, the highlight. But don’t sleep on the seafood, which was also delicious.

One of the best parts of the Dip, as it’s affectionately known, is its location right on the beach. Guests can access the stretch of beach directly adjacent to the property. But it’s not a private beach, so you might encounter crowds.

I didn’t spend any time on the beach itself — it was extremely windy while I was there — but the hotel’s resort fee includes amenities like a beach lounge (umbrella not included), a daily one-hour kayak or paddleboard rental, and beachfront yoga classes.

If you don’t want to get sand everywhere, you can head to one of the three pool options: the adults-only Solara pool, the family-friendly lagoon pool and the Verandah Social Club for those 21 and older (requires paid access).

The family-friendly lagoon spans the length of the property and runs beneath the Solara pool. It also has its own hot tub.

I spent an afternoon in a cabana at the Verandah Social Club, which has some smaller plunge pools and a hot tub.

I appreciated the attentive service from the staff there, who constantly checked on whether guests needed anything.

If you’re looking for other ways to stay active, head to the two-story fitness center, featuring a variety of equipment like free weights, exercise bikes, a rowing machine and treadmills.

Next door, you’ll find the spa and wellness center. I had a relaxing massage that incorporated hot stones and aromatherapy.

The locker rooms come with a sauna and steam room, although I wished there were more amenities like a hot tub and cold plunge.

One of the resort fee inclusions is complimentary high-intensity interval training workout classes at the gym across the street. I signed up for an early morning class. The instructor was friendly, and it was a great way to start my day.

Other amenities include a complimentary one-hour e-bike rental each day, as well as a kids’ club with various activities (but drop-off fees apply).

I had a fantastic stay at this resort, but I’d recommend it for a specific traveler.

If you’re planning to stay on-property your entire trip, it’s a great option. That’s probably why it’s such a popular convention hotel, since everything you need is easily accessible.

I loved the hotel’s design, including the jungle-like atmosphere in the lobby, and I found the dining options to be tasty, albeit pricey.

But if your trip revolves around visiting Miami attractions, you’ll likely want to stay closer to the action.

#3054. Here's What $1,000 Invested at Anthropic's IPO Price Is Worth Now

It was a rough day for Anthropic shares, but not for its IPO investors.

By John Bromels – Nov 19, 2026 at 6:12PM EST

10 stocks we like better than Anthropic ›

As the trading day neared its end, all eyes were on Anthropic (ANT +17.07%)stock. Would the market's newest IPO (not to mention the largest IPO in history) stage a late rally and finish the day above $100/share?

At 3:30 p.m., it didn't look promising. A midafternoon rally that brought the stock price to $99.62/share fizzled, sending it tumbling back down below $95/share again. But then, at about 3:45 p.m., just 15 minutes before the closing bell, things started moving.

Anthropic's share price climbed back above $95... then to $96... and $97...

But then time ran out. The AI heavyweight's shares finished their IPO day at a closing price of $97.17/share, after opening at $111.50/share.

Here's what that means for investors who bought $1,000 of the company's IPO shares and for those who waited.

Although Anthropic announced its official IPO price of $83/share last night, we didn't know what its market debut price would be. That's because the IPO price only applies to designated IPO shares, which are allocated to specific individuals and institutions before public trading ever begins.

If demand is high -- which, of course, was the case for the highly anticipated Anthropic debut -- shares will begin trading at a higher price than the IPO price. This is exactly what happened with SpaceX's (SPCX -3.53%)recent IPO, which was priced at $135/share, but debuted on the NASDAQ at $150/share.

In Anthropic's case, it looks as though that debut price of $111.50/share (a 34.3% premium to its IPO price) might have been a bit too optimistic. Immediately after shares started trading at 11:51 a.m., the price dropped sharply. By noon, it had already tumbled below $106/share. Within the first hour, it fell below $100/share, and stayed there for the rest of the day.

But although it closed well below its debut market price, it was above its IPO price.

$1,000 would have bought you about 12 shares of Anthropic stock at the $83 IPO price (you'd've had $4 left over).

At a closing price of $97.17, you'd have made a one-day profit of $14.17/share, or $170.04 for 12 shares, meaning you'd have $1,170.04 (or, if you bought a fractional share with that last $4, you'd have $1,170.72). That's a 17% gain in one day: not too shabby!

On the other hand, if you missed out on the IPO, but instead bought $1,000 worth of shares right when they debuted at $111.50/share, you'd have been able to afford about 9 shares (8.97 shares, to be exact).

At a closing price of $97.17, you'd've lost $14.33/share today, or about $129 in total ($128.54, if you'd bought exactly 8.97 shares).

So, of your $1,000, you'd have $871.46 remaining, a 14.3% loss.

Meanwhile, if you'd waited to buy shares on the open market until after 1:00 p.m. today, when the worst of the sell-off was already over, you would have bought at a price somewhere between $92.72/share and $99.62/share, meaning you'd have between a 2.5% loss and a 4.8% gain. That translates to a median gain of 1.15% on your $1,000, giving you $1,011.50.

That's not much, but on a day when all the major indexes were down more than 2%, it's not a terrible return for a few hours' investment.

Of course, smart investors don't just calculate their gains after a few hours, or even a few days. Instead, they keep their money invested over the long term, measuring success in years, if not decades.

Given the lack of public information we have about Anthropic's operations and financials, there's no way to know where its share price will end up in three to five years.

So, while IPO investors can pat themselves on the back for their early win, they should pay attention to Anthropic's news releases and quarterly earnings reports to get a fuller picture of how their investment is playing out over time.

#3052. The Inventory Accuracy Problem Smart Fulfillment Centers Still Need To Solve

Amruth Puppala | Senior Engineering Manager | Walmart.

​Walk into a modern fulfillment center, and you will see how much warehouse operations have changed. Robots move products, software coordinates thousands of orders and inventory systems track merchandise across receiving, storage and shipping.

Yet, even with these advances, a familiar problem remains.

A system shows that an item is available, but when someone goes to pick it, the product is not there. The inventory record may be correct on paper, but the physical reality is different. What seems like a minor discrepancy can quickly turn into additional searches, picking delays, order reallocation or missed shipping commitments.

This raises an important question. Instead of simply knowing how much inventory we have, shouldn’t we also know how reliable that information is?

Fulfillment centers and distribution centers handle enormous volumes of inventory movements every day. Products are received, stored, replenished, picked and shipped, often through a combination of manual processes and automated equipment.

Even with well-designed systems, discrepancies can occur.

A pallet may be placed in the wrong location. A receiving transaction might be completed before the merchandise is physically verified. Damaged inventory may not be removed from available stock immediately. Sometimes, a picking exception is recorded without the underlying inventory issue being resolved.

Warehouses already have processes to investigate these situations. Cycle counting, reconciliation and exception management are essential parts of daily operations.

However, many discrepancies are discovered only after they begin affecting order fulfillment.

By that point, the operations team is responding to a problem rather than preventing it.

One idea worth exploring is assigning a confidence score to inventory records based on the operational evidence supporting them.

Consider two storage locations, each showing 100 units available. The first location was recently verified, and its last several picking transactions were completed successfully. The second location has experienced repeated picking failures, unexplained quantity adjustments and an unresolved exception.

Both locations show the same available quantity, but they clearly do not carry the same level of operational confidence.

Today, many inventory decisions focus primarily on quantity, location and availability. Adding a confidence score could give warehouse systems another useful signal when making those decisions.

The score would not represent a new inventory balance. It would indicate how much confidence the system has in the existing record.

This could help teams identify which locations need verification and which inventory discrepancies are most likely to affect upcoming orders.

Recent advances in AI create an opportunity to evaluate these signals continuously rather than relying entirely on scheduled checks.

A system could monitor receiving transactions, inventory movements, picking results and adjustment history to identify patterns that deserve attention.

For example, repeated picking failures at the same location might suggest a discrepancy. An unusual sequence of inventory adjustments could indicate a process issue. A location that has not been physically verified for an extended period could warrant additional scrutiny, particularly if the inventory is needed for upcoming shipments.

Rather than treating each event independently, the system could examine the broader history and determine whether further verification is justified.

Newer AI models can also help interpret exception notes and other information that traditional rule-based systems may struggle to analyze consistently. Where cameras or robotic sensors are available, their observations could provide additional supporting evidence.

The important point is that AI should help identify where to investigate, not make inventory adjustments without verification.

Cycle counting is one area where this approach could have immediate practical value.

Most distribution centers already use scheduled counting programs, often based on inventory value, product movement or operational requirements. Those methods are useful and should continue.

However, a fixed schedule does not always account for problems developing during the day.

Imagine a location that reports 100 units in stock. Several picking attempts fail within a short period, but the inventory quantity remains unchanged. Instead of waiting for the next scheduled count, the system could recommend that the location be checked sooner. The priority could increase if those units are needed for orders approaching their shipping cutoff.

This would allow inventory teams to focus attention where a potential discrepancy is most likely to cause operational disruption. It could also help avoid unnecessary checks in locations where recent transactions consistently support the recorded inventory.

I would not recommend introducing another large platform to solve this problem. Most warehouses already generate much of the information needed. The opportunity is to make better use of it.

A practical starting point would be to combine inventory movement history, picking exceptions, recent count results and upcoming order demand.

Simple rules could first identify obvious discrepancies. Machine learning could then help recognize less predictable patterns, while newer language models could assist with interpreting operational notes and explaining why a location has been flagged.

The warehouse management system would remain responsible for inventory records and transactions. Any quantity correction would continue through established verification and approval processes.

For an initial rollout, I would focus on a limited number of high-volume locations and measure whether the approach reduces repeated picking failures, shortens discrepancy resolution time and improves verification productivity.

Accuracy matters, but so does the amount of additional work introduced. If the system generates too many unnecessary checks, it has not solved the underlying problem.

Fulfillment technology has made progress in improving speed, automation and visibility. But visibility alone does not guarantee accuracy.

A warehouse can have a view of its recorded inventory and still make the wrong fulfillment decision when those records do not match physical conditions.

The next opportunity is to make inventory reliability a continuous part of warehouse operations, rather than something evaluated through periodic reconciliation.

The goal is not to eliminate inventory discrepancies. That would be unrealistic in a continuously operating facility. The goal is to recognize problems earlier, direct people to locations and prevent disruptions before they affect customer orders.

#3048. The Semiconductor ETF Is on Track to Beat the S&P 500 for a 4th Straight Year. It Has Never Done That Before.

The last time this chip fund beat the market three years running, the fourth year cost it around a third of its value.

By Daniel Sparks – Nov 19, 2026 at 6:23PM EST

10 stocks we like better than VanEck ETF Trust - VanEck Semiconductor ETF ›

The VanEck Semiconductor ETF (SMH -2.62%) closed on Nov. 17 at $460.10, putting it up around 28% in 2026. The S&P 500 (^GSPC -2.02%) rose about 7% during the same stretch.

With around six weeks left in the year, the chip fund is ahead by about 21 percentage points. If its lead holds through Dec. 31, it'll have beaten the index for a fourth straight calendar year, after winning in all of the last three. It's never strung together four in a row.

The last time it won three straight, the next year went badly. The fund dropped around 34% in 2022, while the S&P 500 lost about 19%.

I checked this using year-end closing prices from Yahoo Finance, with dividends left out throughout. That record begins in June 2000. Today's fund only dates to December 2011, though, when VanEck replaced the Semiconductor HOLDRS trust that had traded under the same ticker.

Either way, the fund's longest run of wins against the S&P 500 is three years. And including dividends doesn't change which years it won.

The two three-year runs look a lot alike. From the end of 2018 through 2021, the fund gained around 254%, versus about 90% for the index. From the end of 2022 through 2025, it climbed by about 255%, compared with about 78%.

Of course, what matters to a buyer is what came next. Every winning run in the data (six in all, including single-year wins in 2003 and 2005) was followed by a year when the fund's price fell. The declines ranged from below 3% in 2015 to the 34% drop in 2022.

And the industry's sales didn't give much warning. Worldwide chip sales hit a record $574.1 billion in 2022, up 3.3% over 2021, according to the Semiconductor Industry Association (SIA). The slowdown came only in the second half, while the fund had been declining since its Dec. 27, 2021, record close.

Then sales dropped 8.2% in 2023 -- the same year the fund gained around 72%. In other words, the stocks moved before the yearly sales numbers did, in both directions.

I think the main difference between 2026 and 2021 is the starting price. The fund finished 2021 only about 2% below its record close, so investors buying at the start of 2022 paid near-peak prices.

This year, the drop came early. The fund's record close was on June 22 at $668.91, up around 86% for the year. It's since lost most of that gain and is about 31% under the record.

Even so, it hasn't ended a single trading day in 2026 behind the S&P 500 on a year-to-date basis. A winning calendar year, in other words, can still hide a fall of around 31%, and the streak says nothing about the price an investor pays.

What's kept the fund ahead is spending on artificial intelligence (AI) data centers.

Showing how strong that spending still is, Nvidia (NVDA -3.30%), the fund's largest holding, posted fiscal third-quarter revenue (the period ended Oct. 25, 2026) of $115.8 billion after the close on Nov. 17, up 103% year over year. Its data center revenue climbed 110% to $107.6 billion, a small slowdown from 117% growth in fiscal Q2. But total revenue grew 20% from the previous quarter, slightly faster than the 18% sequential growth Nvidia posted in fiscal Q2. And management guided for about $130 billion in fiscal fourth-quarter revenue, a period that has an extra week.

These were also Nvidia's first results since Jensen Huang resigned as CEO. CFO Colette Kress is filling in as interim CEO. The fund climbed around 4% in after-hours trading that evening.

Much of the result may hinge on a few stocks. As of Nov. 16, Nvidia accounted for around 17% of the fund's assets, and Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing accounted for about 10%. Its 10 largest holdings, out of 25, accounted for about 69%.

A fourth straight win would be a first for the fund. But the record suggests a streak tells a buyer little about the year after, and the sales numbers gave little warning before the last one ended.

What a buyer gets now is a price around 31% under the fund's June 22 record close, in a group whose largest member just more than doubled its quarterly revenue. I think the fund is worth considering here, maybe added gradually over the next few months. I'd just size any position with a year like 2022 in mind.

Billing for a global tech customer lifted revenue, but losses widened sharply.

By Motley Fool Transcribing – Nov 19, 2026 at 6:24PM EST

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

SharonAI (SHAZ -6.59%) reported significant progress in converting its contracted commitments into operational AI infrastructure, noting that 2026 served as a foundational year for securing capacity and capital. Management reported that the company's execution focus has shifted toward the delivery and customer acceptance of GPU clusters to drive revenue generation. The company stated that it is utilizing secured debt markets to fund its remaining build-out rather than relying on the unsecured debt market. Management indicated that Australia's energy resources and land provide a strategic advantage for scaling sovereign AI infrastructure as global power constraints increase.

Operator: It is now my pleasure to hand the floor over to your host, Ross Barrows, Head of Capital Strategy and Investor Relations at SharonAI. Sir, the floor is yours.

Ross Barrows: Good afternoon, and welcome to our earnings call to discuss SharonAI's operating results for the quarter ended September 30, 2026. Joining me today is James Manning, SharonAI's Co-Founder and Chief Executive Officer, and Anuj Goel, SharonAI's Chief Financial Officer. I'll now take a moment to read the safe harbor statement. During the course of this conference call, we may make certain forward-looking statements within the meaning of the federal securities laws, including statements regarding our expectations, plans, prospects, strategies, future operating results, and financial performance. For more details on factors that could affect these expectations and cause these differences, please see our most recent Form 10-K and Form 10-Q, and other SEC reports filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission, and available on the SEC's website and in the investor relations section of our website. SharonAI undertakes no obligation to publicly update or revise any forward-looking statement, whether as a result of new information or future events. In addition, during this call, we may discuss certain non-GAAP financial measures.

Reconciliations to the most directly comparable GAAP measures and related disclosures are available in today's earnings release and/or on our investor relations website. James, over to you.

James Manning: Hello, everyone, and welcome to SharonAI's third quarter 2026 earnings call. I'm James Manning, Co-Founder and CEO of SharonAI. For Sharon, 2026 has been the year we built the foundations of this business, capacity, customers, and capital. 2027 is the year we expect those foundations to materialize into meaningful revenue. Execution is our number one priority, and we should be measured by clusters being delivered, acceptance of those clusters by our customers, and the associated revenue generation. Today, we want to show you that we are delivering and how that delivery converts into growth. I'll start with why we believe SharonAI is positioned to win, including the role Australia plays.

I'll then cover what we delivered in this quarter and our achievements post-balance date. Finally, how that all builds into recurring revenue, our contracted book, the NVIDIA relationship, and our capacity. Anuj will then take you through our capital strategy, and I will return with a summary before we open the call for questions. I will start with a brief overview for those that are newer to the story. SharonAI is a leading Australian neocloud. We design, own, and operate the infrastructure that AI runs on. We enable large-scale training, inference workloads, and other high-performance computing, which we deliver through our platform, combining GPU as a service, an AI inference layer, and high-performance storage as one.

Our target customers span hyperscalers, AI natives, leading AI labs, enterprise, and government. We have disclosed some of our customers, which include NVIDIA, ESDS, Canva, and GMI Cloud. We also describe the profiles of other customers we serve, including a global services company, a global technology, a global AI lab, and a U.S.-based inference provider. How will SharonAI lead the pack? I would point to four things. Our NVIDIA preferred partner status gives us priority access to GPU allocations, and we have been working with NVIDIA since 2021, which gives us a natural advantage in our deeper understanding of why and how AI compute workloads work.

Our networking, storage, and orchestration are purpose-built for AI, which supports higher density than traditional cloud environments. Our model is capital-light and faster to market. We deploy into grid-connected Tier III and Tier IV partner data centers under multi-year contracts, which avoids build costs and long lead items like substation and power transmission. Finally, our infrastructure is hosted onshore in Australia and New Zealand with reliable and increasingly renewable energy. Each of those advantages matters more as this market matures, and that is the theme of the next few slides. It is worth looking at the market opportunity and why we are building Sharon the way we are.

Structure Research shows neoclouds like Sharon, which specialize in GPU-based services, gaining a share across every layer of the AI infrastructure. On IT infrastructure, neoclouds made up about 2% of the total IT infrastructure in 2025. However, by 2031, that share is projected to reach over 12%. Within the cloud infrastructure space, the neocloud share is forecasted to roughly triple to about 16% by 2031, while the value of that share, as shown in the middle chart, is forecasted to grow roughly 18x from about $27 billion to over $480 billion. Finally, on AI capacity, neoclouds held about 14% of AI capacity in 2025.

By 2030, however, that share is projected to reach approximately 33%, while hyperscaler share fall from about 81% to below 60% over the same time period. Put simply, demand for AI compute is growing faster than hyperscalers and the legacy market can build on their own, and growing our share of that capacity is moving to neoclouds. That is the market SharonAI is built to serve. The constraint out there is the ability to deliver this performance-focused infrastructure for the AI age, the power, data center, and GPU capacity all coming together, which is what we are focused on at SharonAI. Our framework for what it takes to win in this market has not changed.

We think about GPU allocation, power, regulation, and capital and talent. This quarter, I want to spend some time on power, because it is the constraint we hear the most about from customers and investors, and it is where Australia and our model stands apart. Globally, one of, if not the hardest parts of delivering AI compute is connecting it to power. In most markets, new grid connections, substations, and transmission lines carry multi-year lead times. Our model seeks to avoid these by design.

Every site we deploy into is either an established data center facility that is already connected to the grid, or a new build or the expansion of the existing site where power is already established in that location. Recently, David Burns, our COO, set some of this out in a blog post available on our website. He talked about grid power already being in place, the remaining step to get operational, generally sitting at the data hall level, and where our co-location partners are energizing individual halls. We work with a portfolio of data center providers who are commissioning Tier III and Tier IV data center facilities across multiple sites, so that no single energization determines our overall capacity.

What does this translate into? At all of our sites, we know our contracted customers and when power is on site, with no reliance on future grid utility connections or upgrades. This helps us have confidence in our customer delivery dates. In a market where this is constrained, a credible delivery date is a competitive advantage. On other constraints, our NVIDIA partnership continues to support GPU allocation, and we continue to extend our sovereign footprint in Australia. Regarding capital and talent, we have secured approximately $2.6 billion since December last year, and we continue to strengthen our Board and leadership team with high-quality additions. Why Australia? Australia is so well-positioned to capitalize on the global AI infrastructure build-out.

Global demand for AI compute is outpacing the physical infrastructure needed to deliver it, and timely access to power is increasingly the binding constraint. We believe Australia has the foundation to become a global exporter of AI compute and tokens, and SharonAI is built to take advantage of that. Australia has abundant land, significant energy resources and available power, strong water security, and strong potential for renewable energy at scale. We are close enough to the rest of APAC, but far enough away to be safe and secure. Finally, we have strong connectivity, which ensures low latency delivery as capacity is built out. With this, we are also seeing a change in where compute locates.

Traditionally, we saw a focus on data center proximity to metro regions, and broadly, cloud computing could be defined by the saying that you bring the power to the compute. AI factories are increasingly characterized by the compute going to the power, however. This shift sees the future AI factories co-located closer to power assets, partly due to this scale requirement, but also due to potential impacts on infrastructure and the local environment. These strategic advantages matter as much to our customers. They know they have a stable government and supportive policy environment, a skilled workforce and world-class research institutions, and strong global connectivity and trusted international relationships, including Australia being part of the Five Eyes alliance.

For sovereign and regulated workloads, that is a combination that is difficult to replicate. Domestic demand is also growing quickly. Australian operational data center capacity is forecast to grow from about 1.6 GW in 2026 to about 3.9 GW by 2030, according to Data Centers Australia. SharonAI stands to provide a meaningful amount of this AI factory capacity over time. Finally, on social license. We are also clear that social license is key. Building AI infrastructure in regional Australia depends on meaningful community engagement and on those local communities sharing the benefits, such as jobs and investment.

That is the opportunity that SharonAI was built for, rapidly deploying trusted, sovereign AI infrastructure in a country with the power, land, and stability to do so at scale. Now to the quarter ahead. Let me give you the headline numbers first, and then we will unpack them. 212 MW of total secured AI factory capacity across Australia and New Zealand, of which 129 MW of that is contracted under multi-year take-or-pay agreements. 68,000 NVIDIA GPUs across 2026 and 2027 to be deployed. This quarter was all about converting that position to delivered capacity. Most importantly, we are delivering.

The initial deployments of our global technology customer, a 1,000 cluster, was accepted in August, and the first tranche of that has been billing since the third quarter. Approximately 30 MW of our contracted capacities is expected to be billing from January 2027, representing $400 million-$450 million of annualized run rate revenue. That customer acceptance matters beyond the revenue it brings. It is independent confirmation from a global technology company that we can deliver at scale, and is also the reference point for today's conversation with future customers. $2.6 billion of capital since December 2025, including our first GPU-backed debt facility just last month.

This was our inaugural $356 million fixed-rate GPU-backed debt facility, which shows our ability to execute in debt capital markets. 9.6 billion of cumulative total contract value, which is up around seven times since the first quarter of this year. During the quarter, we signed a $1.32 billion five-year take-or-pay agreement with a global AI lab. Since the quarter end, we have signed a $170 million four-year take-or-pay agreement with a U.S.-based inference provider. A $1 billion five-year take-or-pay agreement with a global services company, with a 30% deployment. We also strengthened the underlying business environment. On the security front, we achieved a SOC 2 Type II attestation.

In operations, we completed NVIDIA Infrastructure Service Testing, or NVIS, verification on all live deployments. With our partners, we announced partnerships with VAST Data and Rafay, which we will come back to shortly. Finally, and importantly, our team. We strengthened the team to ensure that the business behind all of this grows. David Burns joined, formerly from Telstra Enterprise, as our COO. Anuj Goel, former Head of Technology APAC from Macquarie Capital, joined as our CFO. Melissa Anastasiou, former General Counsel at Spark, joined as our CLO. Guy Wylie, former Head of Finance and Treasurer of Telstra, joined as our Head of Capital and Strategy. So what does this all translate into?

Today, we will introduce an annualized run rate revenue, or ARR, into our reporting metrics. We believe that this starts to reflect a material change in our business and gives investors better insight to what is coming for SharonAI. In September 2026, our ARR was approximately $50 million. With the going live of the ESDS and global technology company deployments underway, and expected to be fully deployed and billing in January 2027, we anticipate that ARR will step up to between $400 million and $450 million, or eight to nine times the September level. That step-up relates to about 30 MW, or 23% of our contracted 129 MW capacity.

It is the first of many meaningful steps, and the balance of our contracted capacity comes into billing in stages throughout 2027. We expect a project-level contribution margin of more than 80% at full deployment. That is the earnings power of this business. Contracted capacity with known billing dates, take-or-pay terms, and strong margins. Every deployment we bring through to customer acceptance adds to it directly, which is why delivery is our focus. It is why we are focused on execution. In doing this, we plan to disclose more component timing for investors to understand where we are operationally.

For our global technology customer, for instance, tranche one, which is around 20% of the GPUs in that contract, has been installed and tested, accepted by the customer, and commenced billing in the third quarter. Tranche two, which is the remaining 80% or so of the GPUs, the data hall is ready for service and installation is complete. Testing is in progress, with customer acceptance expected in December, and billing is expected to commence from January. Turning to contracted revenue, this chart shows the cumulative contract value, or TCV, at the end of each quarter this year, and as of today.

We had $1.3 billion under contract at the end of the first quarter. That grew to $7.1 billion at the second quarter, $8.8 billion at the end of the third. As of today, November 16th, contracted TCV stands at $9.6 billion, about seven times where we started the end of Q1, with this TCV only including the four flights of the NVIDIA AICP program for 40,000 GB300s online in 2027. That $9.6 billion is spread across a diverse customer base, from AI labs to hyperscalers, large technology companies to inference providers and enterprise. We will walk through those relationships on the next slide. Together, these contracts give us multi-year revenue visibility as we bring new capacity online.

Looking at the revenue by customer, we will now take a breakdown of the total contract value, or TCV, by customer, and in the order we signed them. Canva and GMI around $40 million. ESDS at $1.25 billion. A global technology company at $950 million. The NVIDIA AICP program anchor at $4.88 billion. A global AI lab at $1.32 billion. The most recent U.S. inference provider at $170 million, as well as the global services company for another $1 billion. Let us take some insights from those contracts. The contract we signed with the U.S.-based inference provider in November was at $19 million per megawatt per year. This matched the highest pricing in our book to date.

The global services company contract, which also signed since quarter end, is priced at $18 million per megawatt per year. What this shows us is sustained contract wins with long-term duration at these higher prices. We have also seen customer deposits increase from 10%-20% of TCV for the beginning of the year to up to 30% of TCV or 60% of CapEx this quarter. We are focused on the quality of the contracts. The size of our book matters, but so does its quality, and in particular pricing, which has strengthened throughout the back half of this year.

Over the course of 2026, we have seen pricing on long-term contracts, which average approximately five years in duration, strengthen and move to more than $19 million of annualized revenue per megawatt, as you can see the contract by contract on this slide. The biggest upside isn't priced in yet. With the NVIDIA AICP program capacity, we expect to sign shorter duration contracts at over $30 million per megawatt. This is the benefit of a book with an ability to take on large portion of shorter term contracts. Our view on the broader market is that pricing reflects two things.

Demand for large clusters with near-term delivery continues to run well ahead of supply, and we can offer customers capacity where power is already secured, which is increasingly scarce. Pricing at these levels, combined with our margins above 80%, is what drives those returns for shareholders. We expect paybacks on our deployments to be well within the life of the contracts that support them. That discipline we apply to every deployment. We commit to GPUs against signed take-or-pay contracts, and we finance them against those contracts.

With approximately 155 MW of data center capacity in Australia available for sale throughout 2027, including both the uncontracted capacity and NVIDIA AICP capacity to be onsold, we have room to sell into this strong pricing environment. It is worth spending some time to update the market on our AICP program. The NVIDIA AICP compute program was signed in Q2 of this year. It's 72 MW and approximately 40,000 GB300s with a six-year term.

The data center is expected to come online and begin commissioning in first quarter of 2027, with the data hall ready for service and NVIS testing in the second quarter and customer billing to commence as part of the capacity of the third quarter build and building throughout the fourth. As a reminder of how the anchor works commercially, NVIDIA's six-year take-or-pay commitment underwrites the 72 MW and approximately 40,000 GB300s. That contracted and anchored revenue gives lenders greater certainty, which lowers our cost of capital throughout the build-out. We can then onsell or upsell that capacity to end customers seeking shorter duration compute at the prevailing market rate.

When we do, we retain 100% of the anchor price and share any upside with it alongside NVIDIA. When you look at the NVIDIA contract on a per megawatt basis, the anchor price is the minimum we will earn on that capacity. Given the shorter term pricing I described moments ago in the market, we expect to place much of it into at materially higher prices. This is the large upside in the TCV which isn't in the market yet and capacity. Turning to capacity as a whole, we announced AI factory capacity, which has grown roughly four times this year from 54 MW in February to 212 MW today, with 129 of those megawatts contracted customers.

We've talked about not waiting on new grid infrastructure to deliver contract capacity. The sites we announce have secured power. The remaining work sits at the DC build, the data hall level, and is spread across both partners and sites, all designed to reduce and mitigate our deployment and development risk. I touched on the SOC 2 achievement earlier on, but security is the other foundation that enterprise and government customers look for. This quarter, we achieved SOC 2 Type II attestation. An independent auditor has tested our security, availability, and confidentiality controls across our AI cloud platform, which operated over a sustained observation period.

Many of these customers require third-party attestation before they can contract, so this matters commercially as well as operationally. Next, we are working towards our ISO 27001 certification, the international standard that government and global customers expect. All of this is about ensuring that we have developed a world-class platform designed to deliver regulated and secure workloads for our customers. The last slide for me, but now based on our partners. Our partner ecosystem has been critical to our success to date, and it's what makes our capital-light model possible. We orchestrate compute, data centers, networking, the data platform, integration, hardware life cycles around a single SharonAI platform, rather than owning every layer ourselves.

Our two platform partnerships are worth highlighting this quarter because both bear directly on how we scale. The first is VAST Data. In June, we committed to deploy 600 petabytes of VAST AI Operating System as the data foundation for our AI cloud. This is one of the largest sovereign AI data deployments in Asia-Pac. On VAST's benchmark of around six petabytes per 1,000 GPUs, that is the data center capacity support the needs of around 100,000 GPUs. Storage should not become the bottleneck as our GPU fleet grows. This quarter, we also launched DataEnclave with VAST, which brings leading AI models into a customer-controlled infrastructure.

Anuj Goel: Thanks, James. As this is my first results call with SharonAI, I'll take the opportunity to say it's a privilege to join the team at this stage of the build-out. In addition, we have and/or will be receiving customer deposits of approximately $800 million as we deploy.

Our approach is to match each source of funding to the stage of our company's growth. Equity and convertible debt funded the platform and our early deployments. GPU deployments are funded with asset SPV-level debt, secured against the GPUs and the contracts they serve. Let me be direct on one of the questions we hear the most from investors. SharonAI is not reliant on the unsecured debt market. The remaining build-out is being funded in the secured debt markets. That is, we will raise SPV-level debt facilities against signed take-or-pay contracts, and that are secured by the GPUs dedicated to them. This is all alongside the capital we've already raised and the customer prepayments we will receive.

The GPUs dedicated to a customer contract sit in an SPV, and the security package comprises those GPUs and the take-or-pay cash flows from that contract. We also provide a temporary parent guarantee that applies until we achieve customer acceptance.

The facility size to the compute dedicated to signed contracts. This is why the secured market is relevant for us. For a business with our contract profile, the secured market is deep and far more open than the unsecured market, and the terms of our first facility reflect that. Interestingly, customer payments or deposits are also a funding source under our contracting model.
