#3046. Beyond Tokens: Why Intelligence Per Watt Is The Metric That Matters

By Dr. Steven Woo, fellow and distinguished inventor at Rambus.

​AI progress centers on tokens: tokens processed, tokens generated, tokens per second and tokens per watt. And because tokens are easy to count, they’ve become the default unit of AI performance. But token-based metrics are only part of the story and miss what users really want. A more useful metric, and one closer to the industry’s goal, is how much intelligence a system delivers per watt.​

“Intelligence Per Watt: Measuring Intelligence Efficiency Of Local AI,” published in November 2025 by a Stanford team, found that small local models can accurately answer 88.7% of single-turn chat and reasoning queries. Intelligence efficiency—capability delivered per watt—improved 5.3 times between 2023 and 2025, roughly 3.1 times from better models and 1.7 times from better hardware—factors that compound rather than add. This efficiency, not pure token throughput, will determine how well AI can keep scaling.​​

Ask a CFO, CIO or CTO running AI workloads what worries them, and it’s rarely whether they’re generating enough tokens. Although tokenmaxxing has become a metric that some companies use to measure AI engagement, others see the dangers of simply measuring token consumption independent of productivity and delivered value. Several companies are cutting back on token spending, with Uber among others stating in May 2026 that it had already spent its 2026 AI budget, and their COO adding it was becoming “harder to justify” their internal AI costs. There’s a growing call for valuemaxxing, which directs teams toward measurable outcomes based on the value being generated by these tokens.​

Concerns about measuring token usage are compounded by the fact that reasoning models don’t produce a single response per query; they work through an internal chain of intermediate tokens the user never sees. Published work on model development puts these generations in the thousands to tens of thousands of tokens. That means a query can consume far more resources than its visible output suggests.​

The pressure to continuously improve value and reduce the cost per token extends beyond inference bills. TrendForce expected server DRAM contract prices to rise 13% to 18% quarter over quarter in Q3 2026, so memory, one of the critical workhorses for AI processing, is getting more expensive as it’s being asked to do more.​​

For hardware companies, that changes the questions being asked. It stops being how many tokens a chip can generate and becomes how much bandwidth memory can deliver per dollar and per watt, and how these metrics will improve in the future.​

For decades, the semiconductor industry relied on Dennard scaling to improve power efficiency. As transistors shrank, they drew less power, so more compute arrived without a matching jump in energy use. That relationship broke down in the mid-2000s as transistors continued to shrink, but the automatic power benefit that used to come with each new process node no longer followed.​

With this lever gone, the industry had to substitute architectural changes for what used to be a by-product of process scaling. Memory is where much of that effort is going: Moving data is a major consumer of system power, making it one of the largest levers to pull.​

The case for stacking DRAM directly on top of a processor has been argued for years. The energy needed to move a bit scales with distance. A DRAM stack beside a processor sits 10 to 12 millimeters away. But stacking the DRAM on top of a processor cuts the distance to about a millimeter. Bandwidth improves separately: Memory beside the processor feeds data through the die’s edges, so interconnect scales with perimeter; stacking can move data through the whole face of a die, allowing bandwidth to scale with area.​

Stacking DRAM has become a focus topic of the semiconductor industry. At Hot Chips 2026, Samsung released more details about zHBM, which places the processor beneath the DRAM stack and claims roughly 70% lower I/O power than the previous generation. That’s what more bandwidth per dollar and per watt looks like.​

Stacking has manufacturing and engineering challenges. Although silicon conducts heat reasonably well, a stack of DRAM sitting on a hot processor acts like a blanket and prevents heat from being moved away. Samsung’s answer is thinner dies and smaller four-high stacks rather than the 12-high or 16-high configurations conventional HBM supports. The energy saved on data movement is coupled with less thermal resistance to achieve a high performance, thermally viable architecture.​

The same constraint is reshaping infrastructure above the die. Enterprise racks that once drew 20 to 30 kilowatts are heading toward hundreds of kilowatts, and eventually toward a megawatt. Power Electronics Magazine reported in January 2026 that 54 volt in-rack distribution “isn’t designed to support the megawatt-scale racks,” and that the transition to 800 volt DC begins in 2027. Copper is expensive and limits current, so when power demand climbs, voltage is the remaining variable that can rise.​

Delivering the most intelligence for a given dollar and a given watt used to be determined by two scaling trends running together: Moore’s law delivered more transistors per dollar, and Dennard scaling delivered them at lower power. Moore’s law continues, albeit at a slower pace. Dennard scaling doesn’t, so the power portion of that result now has to be engineered deliberately, architecture by architecture.​

The industry has hit walls like this before, and the solution was rarely a single breakthrough. It was a return to fundamentals: measuring the right thing and re-architecting around the real constraint instead of the metric that’s easiest to report.​

For the CFOs, CIOs and CTOs approving AI budgets, and for the hardware and software teams underneath them, the number worth tracking isn’t simply how many tokens a system produces. It’s how much usable intelligence and value these tokens return for the dollars and the watts spent producing them.

#3039. As Power Demand Surges, Energy Is Moving Closer To The Edge

Darren H. S. Tan. Chief Executive Officer at UNIGRID.

​Over the summer, Europe suffered a heat wave that strained its power grids, simultaneously increasing electricity demand and forcing some power plants to shut down.​

This isn’t the first time extreme temperatures have impacted the grid’s ability to deliver power. Many places around the world have experienced record-high or record-low temperatures in recent years, and the demand for heating or cooling reached levels that existing energy infrastructure wasn’t designed to handle. ​

The problem is being made worse by the construction of hyperscale AI data centers, which require massive amounts of electricity and further strain the grid. Completely rebuilding the grid to meet modern demands has proven fiscally impractical for many governments, forcing many places to solve the problem on the local level using distributed generation and storage.

Energy infrastructure across the U.S. and Europe was built over a century ago, when energy needs were much different. ​

Even so, studies have shown that we use only about 40% to 55% of the grid on average, and that’s by design, so it can handle spikes when they occur. But recent extreme weather events and data center demand are causing power needs to exceed even that generous buffer.​

For example, the Electric Reliability Council of Texas (ERCOT), which manages electricity in Texas, has said its interconnection queue currently includes over 1,800 projects totaling 474 gigawatts of power, over five times the state’s record peak electricity demand. Ninety percent of those requests come from data centers. ​

The cost to completely rebuild the grid to meet today’s needs is astronomical, with some estimates putting the total replacement cost in the trillions. Because of the potential cost and the fact that the aging grid is a chronic rather than an urgent problem, it receives patchwork upgrades as needed and as government budgets allow. ​

With a full rebuild out of the picture, several strategies are in play to work within the system we already have. When demand approaches available supply, energy companies offer rebates for reducing usage at peak times, implement peak pricing or, in more extreme cases, resort to rolling blackouts, which are planned outages to alleviate the demand during peak periods. ​

Beyond the grid itself, some areas are reducing their dependence on the centralized infrastructure by moving toward local power generation and storage.

Battery energy storage systems (BESS) can store electricity and discharge it when demand exceeds the grid’s capacity. ​

They are already showing promise in several states, such as California, where battery storage capacity has reached over 21,000 MW, equal to about one-third of the state’s peak demand. Eighty percent of that capacity is represented by grid-connected batteries, but smaller batteries are also enabling residents to increase their own energy storage capacity at home.​

As these batteries become cheaper and more reliable, it’s not out of the realm of possibility that these energy storage systems become a standard household appliance in the future, much like a refrigerator or washing machine is today. They can also play a role in energy needs for small businesses.

Being able to store energy and use it in an emergency is only half the equation. The other half is being able to generate electricity independently of the grid. ​

This isn’t a concept that should be unfamiliar to many, as many organizations and homes already have backup generators or solar panels. Although these methods can keep small businesses and homes powered up, they have their disadvantages. Generators are noisy, pollutive and can be dangerous, while solar has significant upfront installation costs. ​

Plug-in solar is emerging as another option for generating electricity locally that has already seen success in Europe and is starting to gain support in the U.S. as well. Instead of being installed on a rooftop, these smaller panels can be mounted on a balcony or a small section of a yard or business property and plugged into a wall outlet to help power homes and small businesses. ​

These systems cost significantly less than traditional solar and are portable, so people can move them around wherever they’re needed. These benefits open up power generation to a whole new segment of the country: commercial and residential renters alike who might never invest in a hardwired battery system or solar installation.

As energy demand continues to increase, expanding traditional grid infrastructure will remain important, but those projects can be expensive and take years to complete. Distributed generation and storage offer another way to increase resilience in the meantime. ​

By generating and storing more electricity closer to where it will be consumed, communities and business leaders can help reduce their reliance on the centralized grid during peak demand.​

We’re unlikely to solve growing power constraints with any single technology, but as local generation and storage become cheaper and more accessible, they can play a larger role in managing peak demand and making better use of the grid infrastructure we already have.​

In the 2.2% year over year and delivered an operating margin of 18.6%. In spite of much higher fuel costs. These results reflect the strength of Copa's business model. Built on Panama's strategic geographic location, the connectivity and convenience of our Hub of the Americas, a structurally low unit cost base, and a passenger friendly product.

Together, these competitive advantages continue to differentiate Copa and support our ability to generate industry leading financial results over the long term. Demand environment remained robust in the quarter, resulting in higher unit revenues and a load factor of close to 89%. Even as we increase capacity by more than 16%. These results reinforce our confidence in the long term growth opportunities in The Americas and in our ability to continue generating profitable growth in the short and long term. Also remain focused on strengthening the competitiveness of our Hub of The Americas in Panama.

Transition from 6 to 8 connecting banks beginning in March of next year will further enhance connectivity, increase schedule options for our passengers, and improved air purification. At the same time, the rollout of STARLINK continues to advance further improving the customer experience and strengthening our value proposition. I would also like to highlight that in September, Copa Airlines was recognized by Skytrax for the 11th consecutive year as the best airline in Central America and The Caribbean. This recognition reflects the commitment of our entire team to continue delivering a reliable, on time, and passenger friendly travel experience. Now I will turn the call over to Robert who will discuss our operating and commercial results in more detail.

Robert Carey: Thank you, Pedro, and good morning, everyone. Let me begin by reviewing some of the quarter's key commercial highlights. Capacity measured in ASMs increased 16.3% compared to Q3 25. Load factor increased 0.7 percentage points to 88.7%. Passenger yields increased 13.8% year over year, and as a result, our operating revenues increased 31.9% year over year to $1.2 billion. Unit revenues or RASM increased 13.5% 12.6¢. These results reflect strong demand and pricing trends across our network, with both higher yields and higher load factors, allowing us to continue increasing unit revenues while growing capacity at a double digit pace.

Of course, we have also maintained our focus on costs and these results are delivered together with a continued competitive unit cost position. Looking ahead, booking trends continue to be strong, supporting our expectation of higher unit revenues than previously anticipated through the remainder of this year. Consistent with these trends, we have updated our 2026 outlook, which Peter will share later. Turning to our network. We remain on track to launch service to Porlamar, Venezuela next week. With this addition, Copa Airlines will serve 88 destinations in 32 countries across The Americas. Further strengthening the connectivity offered through our Hub of the Americas. On the operational side, Copa Airlines once again delivered industry leading reliability.

During the quarter, we achieved an on time performance of 87.1% and a completion factor of 99.7%. Positioning Copa among the most reliable airlines in the world. Regarding product, implementation of Starlink continues on track with approximately a quarter of our fleet currently equipped. We expect to have full implementation across the Copa fleet by mid 27. Regarding our fleet plan, we expect to take delivery of 1 additional Boeing 37 MAX 8 before the year end. Looking ahead to 2027, we currently receiving 12 Boeing 37 MAX 8 aircraft and retiring 2 Boeing 737-700 aircraft ending 2027 with a fleet of approximately 142 aircraft.

This outlook is based on our current order book and remains consistent with Copa's long term growth plan. Of course, as you are all aware, Boeing has announced they will maintain rate 47 for the first half of 27 creating risk of delivery delays. At this point, we have not received notification of any delays. Given our delivery schedule next year, our expectation is that while delays may impact the fleet count at year end, we do not currently anticipate significant impact to our capacity plans for the year. And with that, I will turn the call over to Peter, who will review our financial performance and outlook in greater detail.

Peter Donkersloot Ponce: Thank you, Robert, and good morning, everyone. Let me begin with our financial highlights. We reported a net profit of $176 million or $4.29 per share. Representing a 2.2% increase in earnings per share compared to the third quarter of 2025. Operating income totaled $224 million an increase of 5.7%. Compared to the third quarter of 2025. Resulting in an operating margin of 18.6%. Net margin for the quarter was 14.6%, a 4.4 percentage points decrease year over year. Despite all in average jet fuel price increasing 61.5% year over year, strong demand and higher yields enable us to recover approximately 86% of the increase in fuel-related expense in the quarter through higher revenues.

As a reminder, our fuel recovery calculation compares the year over year increase in revenues attributable to higher RASM with the year over year increase in fuel expenses resulting from higher all in jet fuel prices. Both calculated using 2026 capacity levels. Unit cost excluding fuel or ex fuel CASM increased 1.1%. Year over year to 5.7¢. The year over year comparison in xFuel CASM was impacted by a benefit recorded in the third quarter of 25 related to the extension of 1 leased aircraft. As well as an $8.3 million benefit recorded in the third quarter of 2026 related to an increase in the discount rate used to calculate the present value of expected end of lease cost.

Adjusting for both items, ex fuel CASM would have increased approximately 1.7% year over year, mainly driven by the appreciation of certain Latin American currencies. Turning now to our balance sheet and liquidity. We ended the quarter with $1.6 billion in cash, short term and long term investments, representing 38% of last 12 month revenue. Total debt, including these liabilities, stood at approximately $2.6 billion Our average cost of debt is currently 3.8%, with approximately half of it at fixed interest rates. We ended the quarter with a net debt to EBITDA ratio of 0.8 times, In addition, we continue to maintain substantial flexibility to our unencumbered asset base, which includes 1/3 of our fleet and 16 spare engines.

Turning now to shareholder returns. Our Board of Directors ratified the company's fourth quarterly dividend payment of $1.71 per share payable on December 15 to all shareholders of record as of November 30. Now, turning to our full year outlook. While demand trend across the network continues to be strong, fuel prices have increased relative to the prior outlook assumptions. And as such, we are now expected full year operating margin in the range of 16% to 17% with capacity growth of approximately 14.5%. This outlook assumes a load factor of 87.5 RASM in the range of 12.3 to 12.4¢, ex fuel CASM of 5.8¢, and an all in fuel price of $3.90 per gallon.

Our outlook also includes the estimated $12 million to $14 million impact of the earthquake related disruption at the Tocumen International Airport. Preliminary for 2027 currently anticipate capacity growth in the range of 8% to 9%. Based on our current order book projections and consistent with Copa's long term. We currently expect ex fuel CASM to be in the range of 5.7 to 5.8¢. To summarize, demand and revenue trends remain strong. We continue to maintain disciplined cost control, Our strong balance sheet remains a key competitive advantage. And our proven business model continues to position us well to navigate fuel price volatility while generating profitable growth and long term shareholder value.

Thank you, and we will now open the call for questions from the analysts.

We were suffering from the Boeing delivery delays. So everybody was growing probably at twice our rate. So for us, in a way, it is been catching up. We started getting planes last year, and we had the full year effect this year. We have also had a number of planes this year.

Michael Linenberg: Okay. Okay. that is great. Then just a question to Peter. Usually, it happens once, and then that is kind of the new normal. What triggered that? Is it just maybe a higher interest rate regime? Is it. Or is it. Or is it airplanes?? Maybe the value of aircraft are being sort of reset? What drove that? I am just curious. Behind that move there. I know it was only a small benefit, but I am curious.

Peter Donkersloot Ponce: Yes. Sure, Mike. So accounting standards in our case, IFRS requires to peg it in case of Panama. The Panama company to Panama bond. So when the interest rates increase, Panama bond yields increases, we use that number to update it and calculate the net present value. We have thresholds, so we do not update every quarter. We update it when it surpass certain thresholds. And that is what we have to do with this. So it is pegged to the Panama bond yield.

#3028. The Sixers’ performance in crunch-time games is Good, Actually

At first, the Sixers appeared to be headed toward a blowout loss against the Orlando Magic on Wednesday. They were without all three of Tyrese Maxey, Jaylen Brown and Dean Wade (along with Dominick Barlow and Adem Bona), and they fell into a 27-12 hole less than eight minutes into the game. Instead, the Sixers proceeded to outscore the Magic by 20 points over the remaining 40 minutes, sneaking out of Orlando with a 121-116 win.

That was their 11th clutch win of the season, which the NBA defines as a game that gets within a five-point margin with no more than five minutes remaining in regulation. The Sixers are now 11-0 in such games this season, which is by far the best record in the league. In fact, that record in clutch games puts them in rarefied air, as Mike Lynch of Sports Reference shared after Wednesday's win.

Granted, that clearly unsustainable crunch-time record is also fuel for skepticism about how good the Sixers actually are. It's safe to say that their net rating of plus-46.1 in those situations probably won't hold up for an entire season, particularly given that their overall net rating is only plus-2.7.

None of this is breaking news or hard-hitting journalism. It's stating the obvious. The Sixers are running unsustainably hot in clutch situations and will eventually lose one of these games. However, anyone who's using that record to downplay what they've done thus far this season is missing two crucial points.

The new-look Sixers are still developing chemistry with one another. They're figuring out how best to optimize their schemes both offensively and defensively. That very much remains a work in progress over a full 48-minute game, but the fact that they've been able to lock in at the end of games bodes well. That speaks to an attention to detail that Sixers teams in the past have lacked.

Granted, it helps when you have LeBron James orchestrating your late-game offense. But that's also the point. The "who takes the last shot?" questions from the offseason haven't proved to be a concern at all yet. The answer, unsurprisingly, is that the Sixers don't have a designated last-shot taker. All five guys in their starting lineups are legitimate offensive threats, so they've been adept at hunting mismatches and attacking their opponents' weak spots. That is playoff basketball in a nutshell.

Would it be ideal if the Sixers started blowing teams out so they weren't so reliant on crunch time? Of course. Buying their starters extra rest throughout the grind of the 82-game season would be a godsend. However, there's also value in getting this much crunch-time experience in the regular season, particularly for a team that's working to incorporate so many new pieces on the fly.

"You've gotta go through shit," LeBron said in the season premiere of his Mind the Game podcast this offseason. "… Those are some of the moments that we have to be able to go through some real, live battle moments, in the fight, in order to know really who we are and what we want to become. We've gotta peel the onion. We have to."

Being in these close-and-late situations will help the Sixers develop muscle memory that they can tap into later in the season and in the playoffs. They can see which plays worked and didn't work in those gotta-have-it moments. The best teams use the regular season as a lab to experiment so they have as many answers to the test as possible before the playoffs begin.

There's also a psychological component to their crunch-time performance that could pay dividends down the line. The more close wins they rack up, the more belief they'll have in one another no matter the circumstances. They'll begin to believe that no lead is insurmountable and that they can overcome any obstacle thrown in their way.

In last year's playoffs, the New York Knicks overcame double-digit deficits in every Finals game. They were 6-2 in playoff games where they went down by 10 or more points, which was the best playoff record for any team in the 30 years of play-by-play data, according to NBA.com's John Schuhmann. That didn't just suddenly begin in the playoffs, though.

"What you have to respect about the Knicks, you have to put them away every single possession," Miami Heat head coach Erik Spoelstra told reporters after the Knicks overcame a double-digit deficit in the first half of a game last December. "You can't leave anything to effing chance with that team ever. That's what they do. What they have is a will to win, all right."

LeBron and the Sixers have spent all season discussing the need for them to develop championship habits. Their early-season level of crunch-time performance might not be sustainable, but the way that they're playing in those moments matters just as much. Valuing every possession on offense and locking in defensively are non-negotiables for them to accomplish their goal of winning a championship this year.

The added bonus is that by getting off to such a hot start, they've reduced the temperature under Nick Nurse's seat for the time being. Had they stumbled out of the gate like most early-LeBron teams tend to do, Stephen A. Smith and Kendrick Perkins would likely be all over ESPN's airwaves calling for his head.

The Sixers are by no means a finished product. They'd be the first ones to admit that. But learning to win in crunch time despite that bodes well for their long-term outlook, even if it means their actual record is misaligned with their expected record for the time being. (Don't worry, Cleveland, you can still be the reigning NBA Analytics Champions.)

Jumia is betting on operational improvements, including AI automation, and improved monetization to reaccelerate growth rather than relying on discounts to attract customers.

10 stocks we like better than Jumia Technologies Ag ›

On its third quarter of 2026 earnings call, held on Nov. 18, 2026, Jumia (JMIA -8.76%) announced that its adjusted earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortization (EBITDA) loss narrowed 43% year over year to $7.9 million. The e-commerce operator is proving its monetization strategy can shrink losses even as high memory chip costs hurt smartphone supply across Africa. Long-term gains depend on whether management can reignite customer growth without burning cash.

Three takeaways from the call reveal where the business is headed.

Global memory chip price spikes have driven up prices and caused shortages for smartphones and other electronics across key markets. Smartphones serve as the main gateway for new shoppers; hardware price inflation is dampening broader engagement.

Jumia is increasing its gross margins by cutting costs and improving monetization. Management isn't buying top-line growth through heavy promotional discounts. Instead, higher commission rates and expanding retail advertising services are pushing gross margins higher while keeping fixed overhead lean.

External factors, including smartphone supply and cocoa prices, have put pressure on customers. Jumia's management believes its value offering will help it gain market share. The strategy relies on removing user friction and improving software conversion tools rather than increasing marketing spend.

Jumia updated its full-year 2026 guidance because its early Black Friday trends were below expectations, particularly in the Ivory Coast. Management is using headcount reductions and artificial intelligence tools to trim operational expenses. It is improving its pickup station logistics network, expanding international merchant sourcing, and maintaining strict fee discipline to protect unit margins.

If logistics expansion and social affiliate tools reignite order volume, the enterprise can compound value on a leaner overhead structure.

#3022. Johnson & Johnson Delivered 'Immaculate' Prostate Cancer Data at ESMO. Here's Why Investors Should Care

Johnson & Johnson's $3.05 billion Halda bet is already paying off in the clinic.

By Prosper Junior Bakiny – Nov 19, 2026 at 6:45PM EST

10 stocks we like better than Johnson & Johnson ›

Last year, Johnson & Johnson (JNJ -2.04%) acquired a smaller biotech, Halda Therapeutics, in a cash transaction valued at $3.05 billion. The key asset from that transaction was JNJ-6143, an investigational, early stage candidate for prostate cancer. It will take time to determine whether this acquisition was worth it for Johnson & Johnson, but recent clinical developments suggest that the $3.05 billion the pharmaceutical giant spent may have been well spent. Let me explain.

JNJ-6143 is part of an experimental class of cancer medicines called Regulated Induced Proximity Targeting Chimera, which use proteins found in cancer cells to disrupt certain functions those cells need to survive. This approach could lead to much stronger efficacy than existing standards of care for certain cancers. Johnson & Johnson's JNJ-6143 showed the potential of these therapies in a Phase 1 clinical trial, the results of which it presented at the European Society for Medical Oncology 2026 Congress, held in Madrid in October.

The medicine was tested in patients with metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer. Notably, these patients had received a median of four prior therapies, so we aren't dealing with an easy-to-treat cancer. Yet, JNJ-6143 performed extremely well. It led to an overall response rate (the percentage of patients who respond to treatment) of 75% among patients with measurable disease. This data is highly encouraging. Of course, this was only an early stage study. There is a long road ahead before JNJ-6143 earns approval, that is, if it performs well in future clinical studies.

However, this once again highlights the strength of Johnson & Johnson's pipeline. The company has successfully expanded its lineup of approved drugs in recent years, with newer launches such as Imaavy, which treats generalized myasthenia gravis, and Icotyde, a therapy for plaque psoriasis.

These newer launches could help the company overcome headwinds, such as government-led drug price negotiations and patent cliffs, that it will face over the medium term. Over the next five years, Johnson & Johnson should make significant progress across its pipeline, including with JNJ-6143. Johnson & Johnson's innovative abilities are one of the key reasons the stock is attractive.

And it's worth noting that the company's innovative medicines division could perform even better over the long run, given that it has spun off its slower-growing consumer health division and can focus more on its higher-growth pharmaceutical business. Johnson & Johnson's medtech unit adds even more depth and diversification to the business.

Finally, Johnson & Johnson remains one of the best dividend stocks on the market. With its streak of 64 consecutive years of payout increases, the healthcare leader is a Dividend King, or a stock with 50 or more straight annual dividend increases. Income seekers should stick with this stock for the long term.

Brian Gaebe: Thanks, Michael. Turning to slide six, I wanted to highlight how we continue to deliver strong year-over-year growth in our key financial metrics. Brian Gaebe: Thanks, Alex. Slide 12 provides a high-level overview of our capital strategy. By combining preferred capital with seller notes and, when available, lower-cost senior debt, we believe our typical acquisition profile can generate attractive returns after their financing costs. Additionally, the instrument gives us meaningful flexibility in how we manage cash flow in our capital structure.

That can mean deploying capital into accretive acquisitions or retaining cash to strengthen our position in debt financing, including expanding our borrowing capacity. Those benefits can extend well beyond the immediate cash savings. We recognize that paying in kind increases the outstanding preferred obligation, and we will weigh that trade-off through the same disciplined capital allocation framework we apply to other opportunities. #3012. Applying for Spousal Social Security Benefits in 2027? 3 Things You Need to Know.

Spousal benefits have some unique rules that are worth knowing before you sign up.

By Kailey Hagen, CFP® – Nov 19, 2026 at 7:00PM EST

Spousal Social Security checks tend to be a lot smaller than retirement benefits, averaging just $988 in October 2026 compared to $2,092 for retirement checks. But they can still make a meaningful difference to your household's budget in 2027.

Spousal benefits have a few rules that make them different from retirement benefits, and it's important to understand them if you plan to apply for these checks next year. Here are three of the biggest differences you should be aware of.

You must be at least 62 or older to claim a spousal Social Security benefit. But even at this age, you can’t sign up if your partner is not yet receiving the partner's own retirement benefit. If you're eligible for a retirement benefit on your own work record, you may claim this in the meantime. Otherwise, you have to wait for your partner to apply first.

It's important that you and your spouse are both on the same page about when each of you will apply so that you can maximize your household income. If you haven't already talked through your plans, now is a great time to do so before you try to apply for Social Security benefits in 2027.

Spousal benefits are also available to ex-spouses if you were married to a qualifying worker for at least 10 years before divorcing and you haven’t remarried. Your ex's remarriage will not affect your eligibility to claim benefits on the ex's work record.

Benefits for ex-spouses work almost exactly the same as benefits for current spouses, except you don't need to wait for your ex to sign up for benefits first. As long as you've been divorced for at least two years and are 62 or older, you can claim a spousal benefit on your ex's work record, provided it's worth more than your own retirement benefit.

Social Security retirement benefits continue to grow for every month you delay your application until you qualify for your maximum checks at age 70. But spousal benefits only grow until you reach your full retirement age (FRA). This is 67 if you were born in 1960 or later.

Make sure you sign up by this point at the latest, unless you can’t because your spouse hasn't applied yet. If you fail to sign up by your FRA, contact the Social Security Administration right away to get the process started and to see if you qualify for any retroactive benefits.

#3009. Red Cat Holdings (RCAT) Q3 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

Management pulled full-year guidance while pushing deeper into maritime defense.

By Motley Fool Transcribing – Nov 19, 2026 at 7:12PM EST

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

Red Cat Holdings (RCAT -13.78%) reported third quarter revenue of $11.8 million while withdrawing its full-year 2026 revenue guidance due to delayed funding and contract awards. Management stated that the company is expanding its focus toward maritime autonomy through the Blue Ops division and the proposed acquisition of Steyr Motors. The company reported an inventory increase to $127.3 million to support an opportunity pipeline valued at over $2.7 billion across aerial and maritime segments. Operations during the quarter included the consolidation of Teal Drones and FlightWave Aerospace into a single aerial organization to improve manufacturing and sales consistency.

Operator: Greetings, and welcome to the Red Cat Q3 2026 Earnings Call. [Operator Instructions] As a reminder, this conference is being recorded. I'll now turn the conference over to Ankit Hira, Investor Relations.

Ankit Hira: Good afternoon, and welcome to Red Cat's third quarter 2026 earnings conference call. Joining us are Red Cat's CEO, Jeff Thompson; COO, Chris Ericson; and CFO, Christian Morrison. Please note that certain information discussed on the call today will include forward-looking statements for future events and Red Cat's business strategy and future financial and operating performance. These forward-looking statements are only predictions and are subject to risks, uncertainties and assumptions that are difficult to predict and may cause actual results to differ materially from those stated or implied by those statements. Certain of these risks, uncertainties and assumptions are discussed in Red Cat's SEC filings, including its most recent annual report on Form 10-K and other SEC filings.

These forward-looking statements reflect management's beliefs, estimates and predictions as of the date of this live broadcast, November 16, 2026, and Red Cat undertakes no obligation to revise or update any forward-looking statements to reflect events or circumstances after the date of this call. In addition, our comments on the call today contain references to non-GAAP financial measures such as adjusted EBITDA and key business metrics such as annual recurring revenue. Non-GAAP measures should be viewed in addition to and not as an alternative for the company's reported GAAP results.

A reconciliation of these non-GAAP measures to their most directly comparable GAAP measures as well as definitions of the key business metrics referenced and management's reasons for including the non-GAAP measures and key business metrics referenced may be found in the press release. Finally, I would like to remind everyone that this call will be recorded and made available for replay via a link available in the Investor Relations section of the company's website at redcatholdings.com. With that, I'll now turn the call over to Chris.

Christian Ericson: Thank you, Ankit. Good afternoon, everyone, and thank you for joining Red Cat's third quarter 2026 earnings call. The third quarter was an important period of portfolio expansion and operational investment for Red Cat. We continued building the manufacturing, engineering and testing infrastructure required to support a broader family of autonomous systems across the aerial and maritime domains. At the same time, our results show that we have more work to do to convert customer engagement into funded orders and scheduled deliveries to fully recognize economies of scale and fixed cost absorption. We ended the quarter with significant capacity and inventory in place to support anticipated customer demand. At September 30, inventory and prepaid inventory totaled approximately $127 million.

This puts us in prime position to capitalize on forecasted demand while placing focus on disciplined inventory management, production planning and converting customer opportunities into scheduled deliveries. Our priorities are to strengthen warranty performance, align labor and overhead with delivery schedules and optimize throughput as customer orders convert into revenue. For our aerial division, during the quarter, we brought Teal Drones and FlightWave Aerospace together under Red Cat Aerial, creating a unified organization and a single point of engagement for customers across our aerial systems portfolio. Beyond organizational simplification, the combination is intended to improve the speed and consistency of product development, manufacturing, sales and customer support while enabling technologies and customer relationships to be leveraged across multiple platforms.

Efficiencies gained through this new structure effectuated a 10% reduction in workforce and recurring expenses. This structure is intended to strengthen execution across our aerial portfolio as we continue scaling manufacturing and supporting customer requirements. We also introduced TRICHON, a hand-launched, long-endurance vertical takeoff and landing tricopter designed for intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance missions. TRICHON is the first new platform introduced under Red Cat Aerial and expands the mission profiles and customer requirements we can address. Now to discuss our Blue Ops maritime portfolio. Much of 2026 has been about launching Blue Ops and building the foundation required to support a meaningful maritime autonomy business through internal growth and targeted partnerships.

With our expanded portfolio of maritime systems, we introduced a unified naming convention and added new vessels to our offering, the Blue Ops B-Series portfolio of U.S.-designed and built uncrewed surface vessels. The portfolio includes the B-26, formerly Variant 7; the B-18 tactical and one-way attack platform; and the B-39 platform, purpose-built for logistics and persistent maritime defense missions. The B-18 entered sea trials ahead of its original schedule and the B-39 entered low-rate production. Both platforms are available for orders. We also continue building out our 155,000-square-foot facility in Valdosta, Georgia, to support production, integration and testing for U.S. and allied defense customers. Alongside expansion of our portfolio is our expansion into targeted partnerships.

Blue Ops entered a strategic partnership with Florida Atlantic University's Harbor Branch Oceanographic Institute to strengthen development, testing and system integration. This provides access to a secure deepwater facility, direct ocean access and specialized marine engineering resources. We also partnered with HavocAI to integrate collaborative autonomy, software and command and control capabilities across the B-Series portfolio, supporting coordinated multi-vessel operations and joint customer engagement. In addition, our partnership with Sine Engineering is focused on integrating advanced technologies across Blue Ops USVs and Red Cat Aerial's UAVs, reinforcing the cross-platform nature of our strategy. Also to address Steyr Motors, Steyr is not just a company who manufactures diesel engines for USVs.

Red Cat's acquisition of Steyr Motors adds a power systems company to its portfolio. Power Systems. Please let those words sink in for a moment. This is important -- this is important because power is what determines how far and how long an autonomous system can operate. Steyr's engines already propel Blue Ops' unmanned surface vessels, and the same technology extends across the broader autonomy stack, powering manned, unmanned ground and marine vehicles and further extension of autonomous reach through mobile power units.

This partnership is critical -- a critical enabler of range and endurance, extending the reach of autonomous platforms across the maritime, ground and expeditionary domains while strengthening European supply chain resilience, sales and integration across its product lines. Steyr's propulsion capabilities will support the continued development of Blue Ops, while Red Cat's autonomy portfolio and U.S. defense relationships can create new avenues and growth for Steyr technology. We are excited about the momentum we have established and look forward to carrying it into 2027 as we focus on converting a growing opportunity pipeline into funded programs, production orders and customer deliveries.

Our near-term operating priorities are clear: convert customer engagement into funded orders and scheduled deliveries; maintain disciplined inventory and working capital management; advance the commercialization and integration of Red Cat Aerial and the Blue Ops B-Series portfolio; continue strengthening quality, supply chain resilience and program execution. We believe the capabilities and infrastructure are in place to support a meaningfully larger business -- the next phase is about demonstrating repeatable execution, converting pipeline into funded backlog into on-time deliveries and higher volume into better gross margin and cash efficiency. Those are the operating proof points we expect investors and customers to use in measuring our progress. I'll now turn the time over to Christian to discuss our financial results.

Christian Morrison: Thank you, Chris. Red Cat's financial performance for the third quarter of 2026 reflects continued year-over-year revenue growth as we continue building a durable, combat-proven business and investing in the manufacturing capacity, product development and operating infrastructure required to support our long-term growth strategy. For the third quarter of 2026, revenue was $11.8 million, representing an increase of 22% from $9.6 million in the prior year period. For the first 9 months of 2026, revenue totaled $47.4 million compared with $14.5 million in the prior year period, an increase of 227%. The quarterly increase was primarily due to drone deliveries to the U.S. Air Force and other customers, while year-to-date growth reflects increased drone deliveries to the U.S.

Army, the commencement of deliveries to the Japan Ground Self-Defense Force and additional deliveries to other branches of the U.S. military and allied nations. While revenue fell below our expectations, these investments are building the foundation for sustained growth. Our priority is to translate that foundation into consistent deliveries, stronger margins and improved financial performance. We were disappointed that our FANG FPV offering was not selected as a finalist in the Drone Dominance II competition. Our third quarter revenue expectations included anticipated deliveries associated with this opportunity, which did not materialize and partially contributed to revenue falling below our expectations. Nevertheless, the evaluation identified meaningful strengths.

Teal's production capability scored at the very top compared to the field median, and operator feedback placed usability in the 91st percentile with training results as the strongest at the event. These findings provide a foundation for continued development, while the testing identified specific priorities for improvement in low-light operations and subterranean performance. Our focus is on building on those strengths and incorporating the evaluation feedback to enhance FANG's competitiveness. FlightWave's revenue also fell short of our expectations this quarter. We believe strongly in the product's potential, customer demand and remain committed to addressing the development, production and commercialization challenges that have affected its progress.

Through the integration of FlightWave into Red Cat Aerial, we are bringing together resources, technical expertise and leadership to advance our products with a focus on product reliability, consistent execution and customer readiness. As part of that integration, we eliminated overlapping roles and expect those changes to lower our ongoing operating costs. While meaningful work remains, we are optimistic about FlightWave's opportunity to deliver a differentiated capability to U.S. and allied customers and contribute to Red Cat's long-term growth. Gross profit for the third quarter was approximately $0.1 million, representing a 0.6% gross margin compared with gross profit of $0.6 million and 6.6% gross margin in the third quarter of 2025.

The decrease was primarily due to higher inventory scrap at FlightWave, warranty expense, increased returns and unabsorbed manufacturing overhead and labor resulting from excess production capacity. Our improvement efforts at our FlightWave division began in earnest in Q2 and have focused on ensuring we have the right managers in place to lead our FlightWave division while addressing the root causes of scrap and warranty claims and strengthening product quality before shipment. These actions are intended to improve product quality and manufacturing efficiency while preserving our ability to support higher volumes and deliver a reliable product for the warfighter or end user.

Capital expenditures totaled approximately $17.1 million during the first 9 months of 2026, which primarily includes building out manufacturing capacity and operating infrastructure at our 155,000-square-foot Blue Ops facility in Valdosta, Georgia. This facility gives us room to increase production as customer orders ramp. We are proud of what our Blue Ops team has built in Valdosta, and we're grateful to the city, local and state officials in Georgia for their support. Net cash used in operating activities was $156.8 million for the first 9 months of 2026 compared with $52.7 million in the prior year period. This increase was driven primarily by inventory purchases and operating investments, partially offset by accounts receivable collections.

Our strategic investments in future growth remained significant during the quarter. Total operating expenses were approximately $43.5 million compared with $18.2 million in the prior year period, reflecting continued investments in engineering personnel, prototype development and testing, sales and marketing resources and the corporate and technology infrastructure required to support our growth objectives. Operating loss was $43.4 million for the third quarter compared with $17.5 million in the prior year period. Net loss was $40.4 million or $0.26 per basic and diluted share compared with a net loss of $16.0 million or $0.16 per basic and diluted share in the third quarter of 2025.

We are prioritizing spending around existing customer commitments and development programs with the clearest path to commercialization. The integration of our Red Cat Aerial business has provided an opportunity to consolidate overlapping activities and direct resources towards our highest priority programs. Research and development expense increased to approximately $16.1 million during the quarter from $6.0 million in the prior year period. This increase was primarily due to engineering personnel costs at our aerial divisions, prototype development with a particular focus on Blue Ops prototypes, testing and other expenses associated with the development of new and enhanced drone platforms and related technologies. Our balance sheet strength and liquidity position continue to provide us with substantial financial flexibility.

As of September 30, 2026, we held $242.7 million in cash compared to $167.9 million at year-end 2025. Working capital totaled approximately $355.8 million, providing resources to support our operating requirements and strategic growth initiatives. This liquidity gives us flexibility to execute existing programs and selectively pursue opportunities that we believe can create lasting shareholder value. Our inventory strategy continues to be an important component of our growth, production readiness and investment in shorter delivery times. Inventory totaled approximately $117.2 million at quarter end, up from $23.5 million at year-end 2025. The increase in inventory during the quarter was primarily driven by the strategic procurement of key components and materials to support production of our Hellcat ISR drones.

Additionally, inventory levels at our Blue Ops division increased significantly as we prepared for anticipated customer deliveries while establishing appropriate safety stock levels to support production readiness. We remain focused on converting inventory into customer shipments while maintaining disciplined working capital management. We view our balance sheet and inventory position as strategic assets. With approximately $243 million of cash and significant investments in inventory, manufacturing and technology development, we believe we have the financial resources to support future growth opportunities as they emerge. At the same time, disciplined capital deployment and converting those investments into revenue and improved operating performance remains important priorities. Turning to our outlook. We continue to see substantial opportunities across domestic and international markets.

However, since we last provided our full year revenue target, anticipated funding and contract awards have not materialized on the timelines we expected, and the outcome of the Drone Dominance program's Gauntlet II has removed an anticipated contributor to our near-term revenue outlook. These developments have changed both the timing and expected contribution of the opportunities underlying our prior target, and we no longer expect to achieve our previously announced full year 2026 revenue target and are withdrawing that target. Uncertainty surrounding defense funding, customer procurement decisions, customer acceptances and delivery schedules limits our ability to predict the timing and amount of future revenue. Our focus remains on converting opportunities into funded orders and executing on customer deliveries.

Regarding our proposed acquisition of Steyr Motors AG, the acquisition adds an iconic brand to the Red Cat family, an established revenue base, which approximated 60% concentration in defense in 2025 and 2024 and reported an order backlog exceeding EUR 300 million, providing a substantial base of potential future revenue. Steyr also brings accretive gross margins and exposure to additional defense customers and programs. Our investment case centers on growing Steyr's external engine business, complementary synergies and strengthening propulsion capabilities for Blue Ops. We will evaluate success through cash generation, returns on invested capital and measurable operating improvements with particular attention to preserving sufficient liquidity to execute Red Cat's existing programs. Several factors support our long-term growth opportunity.

First, defense and national security customers continue to prioritize affordable, mission-ready autonomous and unmanned systems. Second, our expanded manufacturing footprint, inventory position and product portfolio provide the operational foundation to support higher delivery volumes as orders materialize. Third, our investments and partnerships across Red Cat Aerial, Blue Ops, Apium, HavocAI, Anduril, Sine Engineering and Quaze broaden our capabilities across aerial and maritime platforms, collaborative autonomy, command and control, cross-platform integration and wireless power. We continue to see multiple growth vectors across aerial and maritime autonomy, supported by an expanding product portfolio and continued customer engagement. Our focus is on translating those opportunities into funded orders, deliveries and stronger financial performance.

Market conditions continue to support long-term demand for autonomous and unmanned systems across U.S. and allied defense customers. Combined with our liquidity position, expanded product portfolio and manufacturing infrastructure, we believe Red Cat is positioned to participate in the ongoing modernization of defense technology while remaining focused on execution and financial discipline. With that, I'll now turn the call over to our CEO, Jeff Thompson.

Jeffrey Thompson: Thanks, Christian. Good afternoon, everyone, and thank you for joining us. Christian and Chris have reviewed our third quarter in detail. I will be brief and move on to Q&A. I'm going to review our opportunities going forward for both Red Cat Aerial and Blue Ops. At this time last year, our opportunity pipeline was 0 for Blue Ops. In 1 year, we've been able to prove ourselves repeatedly in exercises, crucibles, live demonstrations, private demonstrations and more. We splashed our first boat last December and 11 months later, we have our first customer. Let's move on to Red Cat Aerial. The Red Cat Aerial opportunity pipeline is approximately $440 million. Most of these are unannounced tenders, so we will not put a number for funded opportunities until we have public acknowledgment of these opportunities by their governments, so we will consider them not funded. We have 4 letters of requests and expect a few more this month. The LORs add up to approximately $100 million. We expect to receive more as the Hellcat continues to perform in theater. Mike Latimore: Got it. And talked about your first purchase order for the B-26. Can you just elaborate a little bit on that? What's the initial use case? And where could that expand?

Jeffrey Thompson: Yes. The approximately $250 million I mentioned is already funded. They don't have to worry about any new resolutions, no new administrations, no NDAAs, no new appropriations. It's about $250 million that is funded right now that we're going after in the United States. And then if you look into INDOPACOM, these are all things you can go look up. There's multiple countries. There's a massive amount that are funded already, and we expect there's -- that are different schedules than our government to also be funded.

So we think that $2 billion plus in INDOPACOM is probably going to expand pretty rapidly through the first half of 2026. But we're just very excited that our boat continues to perform. We couldn't even get a phone call back from these folks when we were trying to get in there 6 months ago. Now after people have seen our boat perform in exercises, private demonstrations. We were the only boat at the Taiwan U.S. Defense Conference about a month ago. We're working with General Flynn, who ran that portion of the Army for 4 years. He's been very helpful with us getting into the right spots for these USVs in the INDOPACOM region.

That region has 7,000 islands, and that number is only going to go up for not only the opportunity pipeline, but for the funded pipeline there.

Craig Irwin: So Jeff, we understand the strategy well of building inventory given the customer demand can spring really quick, and you have visibility on several of these funded programs out there internationally and domestically. Can you maybe just talk a little bit about the breakdown or the relative contribution between Red Cat Aerial and Blue Ops? And then it seems the international markets are working really well for you these days. Is there an opportunity maybe with the new relationships from Steyr to leverage that to accelerate international growth of the Red Cat Aerial operations?

Jeffrey Thompson: Yes, absolutely. We've already been asked to -- from one of the funding partners for Ukraine if we look at that possibility, and we're exploring it so that we would have a made-in-Europe version for that region.

That's about $5 million or $6 million a month for that to do sustainment. All of the LORs talk about replacing Chinese and having NDAA-compliant drones finally in Ukraine. And now you see that FMS is making a comeback and being put onto the UAS marketplace. That will help us dramatically.

I'm in D.C. early next month, we'll be meeting with those folks. So there's a -- we've geared up to really try to crush it in Q4 to just deliver it as soon as we get these things funded.

Christian Morrison: And Craig, I'll add to that a little bit. I mean, between Q2 and Q3, Blue Ops inventory went up 7x. I mean we need safety stock. We need inventory in Blue Ops period. And that 10% of the United States is the U.S. Navy SEALs. So it's already an engine that they love already.

Craig Irwin: Love that. So Chris, you've been spending time in Japan. And I guess this is a group, obviously -- question to the whole group, obviously. But Asia Pac and USVs is a natural fit, right? The analogy of the MQ-9 Reaper, the number that we've lost was never meant to be used in a contested environment, way too expensive, $50 million when you got a $0.5 million ISR drone as an alternative. USVs, the same logic can easily be applied for these navies, particularly of countries that have smaller budgets than the U.S. or some of our allies or European allies, I should say.

Can you maybe talk a little bit about the momentum with what people might not consider Tier 1 buyers, the important allies of the United States across Asia Pacific that really do want to defend their borders and have clear homeland defense and strike capability if necessary. Is this an area of the market that's coming towards you?

Christian Ericson: Absolutely. I mean this is an area of the market that's rushing towards us. And it's exciting. You've got a lot of these groups out there that traditionally had relied on U.S. protection, right? They're relying on the big boys overseas to help protect them, take care of them. We've got large systems that we were able to protect them with. But now as we are telling them, hey, you need to rely on yourself a lot more, they are very interested in what we have to offer. They're taking their learnings from what they're seeing in current conflicts that are out there.

They're not looking back to the conflicts 50, 70 years ago, they're looking at the current conflict and saying, "Hey, can we do more with less? Can we do more with smaller vehicles?" They look at the USVs and they're saying, "Hey, we can have 100, 200, 300 of these taking down a lot more than a single battleship can take down. We can cover a lot more of the water." I mean you think about the water, the area that's over there, there's so much space to take over, to look over. And by having these USVs, especially with our USVs being interoperable with our UAVs.

So launching our drones off of the boat, sending our boats out there, all of our boats, they've got SATCOM communications. They can take on any type of communication with a massive bandwidth and have the birds being controlled right off of the boats, you really expand what you can cover with a smaller price, a smaller cost to what they're traditionally used to or had thought of in the past. And so this has brought in a large amount of interest and a large amount of demand that's been building up.

Jeffrey Thompson: Yes. And Craig, just to add to that -- with those 7,000 islands, that's a lot of area to cover. Some great examples. Even the B-26 can go almost 2,600 miles at slower speeds. The B-39 can be out there for 1.5 months at 7 knots with 10,000 pounds of payload. So the -- what we're building is -- let's back up. We built Blue Ops to be ready for the INDOPACOM region next year. And then the Strait of Hormuz came in and put everything into fast gear, and that's great because we've been able to get invited to all these exercises we weren't initially invited to. As we started winning them all, we got invited to some more.

We just got out of Poseidon's Fury. We're in a lot of other situations we can't talk about. But when you see the statistics, when you have the boat building capability and expertise that we have, we're building boats that do things no one else can do at speeds, distances, reliability, affordability. It's just amazing how quickly we're becoming one of the go-to folks for boat building.

Craig Irwin: Excellent. So last question, if I may, if I could squeeze one in. Steyr, seems that their sales force is probably in all the right places already, particularly complementary to the Red Cat sales force. For USVs and for Red Cat Aerial, how well penetrated are they with the customer base that you're looking forward to the next couple of years?

Jeffrey Thompson: Well, USVs, let's face it, Ukrainians basically invented this newer, more lethal version of it. There was USVs with some of the older companies that have recently been acquired, but they were -- they didn't have the capabilities and the Ukrainians actually proved it with their tactics. But to take something from that era and to put it into a brand-new era that can do all the things that were -- people are asking to be done, to have them as interceptors, to have them as escorts to do all these things way less expensive, no humans, river crossings, all these things, that engine could be in a lot of USV-like situations across the globe.

Also, there are other engines that are not marinized that can be used in tanks like they are already doing. There's just a lot that can be -- there's so much that can be expanded, and that's why we're going to invest into the Austrian facility. And they're probably just touching the surface. The Navy SEALs already love the product. That's the hardest thing when you bring a new engine in, we're not bringing a new engine in. We're bringing in an engine that the U.S. government has already done all the checkups on, gone to their factories, done all the -- checked all the boxes on it.

So we're not starting with a new engine that we got to convince the U.S. military or the DoD to use. So we think that we can do great things together with Steyr.

Craig Irwin: Excellent. Well, we look forward to following your progress. Congrats on almost there on Steyr. It's nice to see that one in the right direction now.

Operator: Our next question comes from Amit Dayal with H.C. Wainwright.

Amit Dayal: So just on the inventory side, guys, I mean, it looks like you do have some confidence that some of this inventory can be used to meet the orders coming up. Is that the right way to look at it? And what portion of inventory do you think you may have to write down?

Christian Morrison: I mean these are not perishable goods, Amit. I mean we're comfortable with the inventory that we're not going to have to take any reserves there.

Amit Dayal: Understood. Okay. That's good to hear. And then post Steyr, I mean, once this closes, et cetera, like, what does the balance sheet look like? And then how do you sort of manage your growth needs with working capital needs just for the organic or legacy Red Cat business versus including initiatives for Steyr?

Jeffrey Thompson: Well, we're already called -- Red Cat is already being called legacy. That's new. I appreciate that. There's a lot of things that we're looking at right now as we need to get to 50 plus 1 before we make any assumptions or give any projections on that. So once we get there, we can get there. And our revenue is increasing with the one big shipment of our inventory, everything changes and our financials look the way we want them to look and everyone wants them to look. So we're very comfortable with where we are right now in the growth.

And once we get that deal done because it does expand our revenue opportunities, and it's already an accretive acquisition.

Operator: Our next question -- our last question for tonight comes from Jonah Henschel with Clear Street.

Jonah Henschel: To begin, you mentioned the Taiwan award in mid- to early March 2027. Where is international demand for your surface vessels building? And what exactly should we look out for that would allow that award to land on time?

Jeffrey Thompson: Well, we are not doing on-time government predictions. Maybe go onto Polymarket for that. It's been stated that the award is in March for 2027 for Taiwan for quite some bit. I think the original budget was $40 billion, they got knocked down by the opposition of $29 billion. So we are not guaranteeing Taiwan's. I think that tender's for 1,320 units. It was 1,600 until they got knocked down because of the going from $40 billion to $29 billion. There are other chunks of Taiwan that are in addition to that. I don't want to go into the details of any of those. We do have a great working relationship with supply chain capabilities there now.

The Hinckley family has been doing business there since 1978 in Taiwan, and Hinckley has done a lot of actually working acquisitions there. So we feel very comfortable that our supply chain and capability to build additional boats there with them is going to put us in a good spot. And having the capability and the way our folks are just purely performing against our competitors, we think we also have a great chance there.

Jonah Henschel: Okay. That helps. And then just a quick follow-up, if I may. Beyond Taiwan, would you mind providing a little more color on where else you're seeing international demand for Blue Ops?

Jeffrey Thompson: From Australia all the way down to Taiwan. You picked the country. Some of -- a lot of the activity we're talking about on the Hellcat and Black Widow is in Korea. We see very significant possibilities with Japan. We're spending a lot of time there with Chris and General Flynn, and we'll continue to do so. They've already started buying our Black Widows. We're hoping to sell more Black Widows in Japan. So I would say Japan and Taiwan, even Japan could even be bigger than Taiwan. So we do not know yet.

Operator: I'd now like to turn the floor back over to Jeffrey Thompson for closing remarks.

Jeffrey Thompson: Thanks, everyone. I have a very aggressive Investor Relations schedule starting tomorrow morning in D.C. and then to the Deutsche Bank Conference on Wednesday. Look forward to speaking to you all. Thank you.

#2997. 1 Unstoppable Stock to Buy Before It Joins NVDA and AAPL in the $1 Trillion Club

AMD looks poised to reclaim a $1 trillion market cap as Nvidia turmoil creates an opportunity.

By Marc Guberti – Nov 19, 2026 at 7:32PM EST

10 stocks we like better than Advanced Micro Devices ›

Advanced Micro Devices (AMD -7.72%) briefly became a $1 trillion company in September, but it lost that milestone after a prolonged artificial intelligence (AI) stock correction. However, the chipmaker is set to rejoin Nvidia (NVDA -3.30%) and Apple (AAPL -0.92%) as a trillion-dollar company. These are the catalysts that can drive the stock higher.

AMD has been viewed as the No. 2 graphics processing unit (GPU) chipmaker for several years, with Nvidia comfortably holding on to the top spot. However, Nvidia suddenly faces significant uncertainty with former CEO Jensen Huang out of the company and angling for a comeback.

Nvidia currently doesn't seem receptive to a reunion, and that can cost the company. Some investors argue that Huang's departure will make it difficult for Nvidia to continue innovating despite the competitive edge it has already obtained.

The AI industry is moving rapidly, and leadership complexities can cost Nvidia valuable time. It can be the difference between missing out on the latest technology and watching hyperscalers turn to alternatives.

This scenario positions AMD as the chipmaker with the most to gain from the confusion, and the company has been taking major steps to close the gap. For instance, AMD is making its chip fleet more attractive by making it much easier for developers to port existing Nvidia CUDA applications to its HIP platform.

Nvidia's CUDA was previously a major moat. Moving to another software essentially meant rewriting vast amounts of code, but that's no longer the case. If AMD can win over more businesses with an easier migration, it creates more headaches for a company already full of them.

Although Nvidia has captured most of the headlines throughout the AI boom, AMD has been quietly accelerating its growth. Data center revenue surged by 97% year over year in the third quarter, while overall revenue reached $13.4 billion, up by 45% year over year. That also represents a 16% sequential boost.

AMD CEO Lisa Su told investors that demand for its AI products is still accelerating. The chipmaker also remains confident that revenue growth will surge in the coming years, along with higher net profit margins.

AMD trades at a 30 forward price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio, which may be higher than what some investors are willing to handle. However, this same company almost doubled its net income year over year. AMD wrapped up the quarter with an 18.2% net profit margin, and if it can get closer to Nvidia's 62% net profit margin, the stock should have an easy time reclaiming a $1 trillion market cap and marching toward new highs.

#2993. Michael Burry Says He Tried to Warn You About Nvidia, CoreWeave and Nebius. Here's What the 'Big Short' Investor Saw

The famed investor took a victory lap as AI stocks slid again on Thursday.

By Jonathan Ponciano – Nov 19, 2026 at 7:43PM EST

Michael Burry, the investor made famous by "The Big Short," isn't shy about saying "I told you so."

"Coreweave, Nebius, NVIDIA, semis, I tried to warn you all," Burry posted on X on Thursday afternoon. "I didn't say short. But I provided the information one would need to sell."

He picked a good day for it. Nvidia (NVDA -3.30%) fell 3.3% on Thursday, CoreWeave (CRWV -6.11%) dropped 6.1%, and Nebius Group (NBIS -9.39%) sank 9.4%, as tech stocks gave up an early rally.

Here's what Burry saw, and what investors should do with it.

Michael Burry. Image source: Getty Images.

Burry's warnings came in pieces. In mid-October, he shared a Wall Street Journal story arguing that CoreWeave's sell-off showed the pressure from rising borrowing costs, adding his own commentary: "Dumb da dumb dumb da."

CoreWeave and Nebius are so-called neoclouds, companies that rent out Nvidia-powered computing to AI developers. Building their data centers takes enormous amounts of money, much of it borrowed, so higher interest rates hit them hard.

On Nvidia, his case is about the long run. He says he expects Nvidia's competitive edge to shrink over the next five years. In September, he also argued that its chips "may be economically depreciating waiting in warehouses while GAAP depreciation remains at zero," meaning the hardware could be losing value faster than the accounting shows.

The numbers have lent credence to his concern. CoreWeave closed Thursday at $44.91, down 76% from highs last year, and Nebius finished at $96.92, down 66% from its June peak. Nvidia has held up better but still sits 39% below its October high. The damage has spread across the chip industry, too: The VanEck Semiconductor ETF (SMH -2.62%), a basket of the biggest chip stocks, is down 33% from its June high.

As he laid out his long-term worries about Nvidia earlier this month, Burry said he imagined "the whole market is going to think this is a heck of a trade fairly soon." But since then, the stock has fallen another 16%.

Nvidia's business, meanwhile, hasn't cracked. Its revenue jumped 103% to $115.8 billion last quarter, and management raised its growth forecast for next year. The stock's slide this month coincided with Jensen Huang's sudden resignation as CEO, rather than a drop in sales.

If you own neocloud stocks like CoreWeave and Nebius, watch how much they borrow and what that debt costs them. If you own Nvidia, watch whether customers keep buying at today's pace, and whether the chips they buy hold their value.

The AI stocks that come out of this sell-off in good shape will be the ones with the best answers to those questions. For long-term investors, that's a better guide than any single post on X, even one from Michael Burry.

Universal Technical Institute (UTI -8.48%) released its final set of earnings for its 2026 fiscal year, and probably wishes it hadn't. The vocational education specialist fell short of analyst estimates, and its guidance also left something to be desired. Investors expressed their displeasure by trading the stock down by almost 9% that day.

That top-line figure was slightly higher than the average analyst estimate of just under $235 million. Pundits tracking UTI stock were also modeling a slightly higher earnings per share (EPS) figure of $0.33.

UTI is in the midst of implementing its multi-year "North Star Strategy," aimed at transforming its historical focus on training for certain vocations into a learning institute for a variety of them. It attributed the dip in profitability to expenses related to this effort.

UTI also proffered revenue guidance for the current fiscal year of $925 million to $945 million.

However, those expenses -- which include spending on four planned new campus openings -- will continue to impact the bottom line. Management is guiding for annual net income of $0 to $5 million ($0 to $0.09 per share), which would be well down from fiscal 2026's $33.6 million. It's also notably below the $0.73-per-share consensus analyst estimate (ditto for UTI's revenue guidance, which whiffs on the $971 million collective pundit forecast).

UTI's expansion plans are ambitious and, in my view, achievable. Demand for vocational education is high given the shortage of skilled professionals in such trades, so this feels like the opportune time to build out an educational business. I think UTI has a brighter future than the Thursday market reaction would indicate.

As of now, the index is about 8% below its October high. The Nasdaq-100 and the tech sector are faring far worse, and investors are thinking about a potential bear market for the first time in over a year.

But if you go back several decades and look at situations like this -- the S&P 500 declining four straight weeks following a record high -- the outlook from here could actually be pretty bullish.

Since 1970, there have been 12 occasions when the S&P 500 has fallen four straight weeks right after hitting a new all-time closing high the previous week. Historically, the short term following these events has been more volatile. But it's the longer-term recovery period that's more meaningful.

Six months after the streak ended, the S&P 500 was higher in 10 of those 12 instances. The median gain was 13.4%, which is more than double the 5.2% median six-month gain during an average week since 1970.

Over the subsequent 12 months, the S&P 500 was higher on 11 of the 12 occasions, with a median gain of 16.5%.

I don't want to over-inflate the success rate here when the sample size is only 12, but I believe there's an explanation for this. Even bull markets have periods when stocks pull back. In many cases, it's not necessarily a sign that economic growth is stalling and a major bear market is imminent. It's just a normal part of the process of investing in risky assets. These are often normal market gyrations, and I think the data shows that over the long term, stocks tend to rise more often than fall.

Data source: Investing.com data and author's analysis of S&P 500 daily closing prices. "Streak ended" is the final trading day of the fourth losing week. Returns are measured from that close. Three months = 13 weeks; six months = 26 weeks; 12 months = 52 weeks.

One month from the streak's end, the chances of a positive return are pretty much a coin flip. It's not until three months out that, historically at least, the odds start to swing in your favor.

But I believe the overall trend is pretty clear and a good example of why a long-term buy-and-hold strategy is usually the best approach. In this scenario, the odds of generating a positive return have historically kept improving the longer you stay invested. That's a good framework to keep in mind whether stocks are steadily declining or near all-time highs.

History suggests that dips like these are much more likely to be healthy pullbacks during longer-term rising markets than a bear market warning.

Therefore, there's probably little need to make any major changes to your investment process. That means keeping your stock/bond allocations intact. Continue investing monthly or with every paycheck. Make sure your portfolio still aligns with your long-term goals.

If anything, you could consider positioning the equity segment of your portfolio a little more defensively. Moving from a core position in the Vanguard S&P 500 ETF (VOO -1.98%) to something like the Vanguard Value ETF (VTV -1.58%) or the Invesco S&P 500 Low Volatility ETF (SPLV -1.27%) could be a smart way to take some risk off the table while maintaining your equity exposure.

Market dips don't necessarily need to be feared. They can also be taken advantage of.
